items.articleBody:
I f you are looking for government corruption, Washington has always been a target-rich environment. But the past two years of the Trump administration have seen the swamp rise to extraordinary levels. Despite remarkable threats from the White House suggesting that congressional investigations [might be a crime](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/us/politics/trump-democrats-congress-oversight-committee.html), Democrats are preparing to scrutinize what Senator Raphael Warnock has called “the most corrupt administration in American history.”

Many Democrats will be tempted to go directly after the president for his misdeeds. A better strategy would be to take a page from the prosecutor’s playbook on investigating organized crime.

In many ways Trump and his inner circle resemble an organized crime family, with Donald as the don. Such groups are tightly knit, held together by bonds of unwavering loyalty to the organization and its authoritarian leader. They prize secrecy. They enforce their demands through intimidation and coercion. The members work to enrich themselves, displaying little regard for law or institutions. Responsibilities are compartmentalized and diffuse, in ways that insulate those at the top from accountability.

When prosecutors work to dismantle these organizations, they often start from the bottom: find the lower-level players, build cases against them, persuade them to cooperate, then work up the ladder.

*[[Quinta Jurecic: A very suspicious prosecution of two former FBI officials](https://www.theatlantic.com/ideas/2026/10/fbi-prosecution/689138/?utm_source=feed)]*

But expecting Attorney General Todd Blanche to pursue such cases would be like expecting the consigliere to investigate the family. He almost certainly won’t appoint special counsels to investigate, even though a squadron of them is called for. And Trump has [already promised](https://www.wsj.com/politics/policy/trump-promises-mass-pardons-to-staff-before-leaving-office-d7274d32) to pardon everyone “who has come within 200 feet” of the Oval Office. Given the zeal with which he wields the pardon power, anyone whose dreams of accountability feature perp walks and orange jumpsuits is likely to be disappointed.

Congress might also be tempted to impeach Trump, as it did twice during his first term. But Democrats would be wise to avoid that route this time.

Presidential impeachment sucks all the air out of the room. It feeds Trump’s martyr complex and keeps him at the center of attention. And although it might satisfy some Democrats, in the end it will almost certainly fail again. In the new Senate, more than 10 Republican senators would have to vote to convict. Even after such a decisive electoral rebuke, it’s hard to see that happening.

The more fruitful course for Democrats will be to leave Trump to his interior decorating and recognize that their time is better spent focusing on the misconduct of those around him and those tied to his administration. In the process, they will inevitably document the misconduct of Trump himself.

Congressional-oversight investigations are now more crucial than ever. In this environment, they are the best available vehicle for exposing and documenting the administration’s misconduct. And unlike with a criminal grand jury, congressional investigations can be open to the public, which is essential for informing the public’s vote, come 2028. Congress can build a public record of the transgressions of this administration, working all the way up to Trump himself, for all of America to see.

T he coming congressional investigations will face unprecedented hurdles. But Congress possesses many of the same investigative tools that a prosecutor would use to build a case against a crime boss and his organization. Congressional committees are busy staffing up with attorneys and investigators, many of whom resigned or were forced out of Blanche’s DOJ, who know how to do this work.

First, as Senator Ron Wyden so succinctly [posted on X](https://x.com/RonWyden/status/2117830246342828496): “Subpoenas.” Like a prosecutor conducting a grand-jury investigation, Congress can compel the production of documents and the testimony of witnesses under oath. While in the minority, Democrats could only request information, and had no way to force compliance. That will now change.

Congress, like a prosecutor, also has the power to grant immunity to a witness who claims a Fifth Amendment right not to testify. For a witness, a grant of immunity is an offer you can’t refuse: It requires you to testify or face contempt charges. As a former federal prosecutor, I’ve seen firsthand the power of immunity in unearthing the truth.

Congress is often reluctant to grant immunity for fear of undermining a potential criminal prosecution of the immunized witness. But that is less of a concern if one assumes that Trump will pardon the witness anyway.

If people defy subpoenas, Congress can go to court to enforce them, and it should do so aggressively, asking judges to fast-track the process. Courts can move quickly when they need to. Stonewalling should not be tolerated or rewarded.

Although we can expect the administration and those closest to Trump to resist at every turn, private companies and individuals have a great deal of relevant information and will likely be more compliant. These are the lower rungs on the ladder that can lead to further evidence and investigation.

Congress can also vote to hold witnesses in contempt. Under current law, a contempt resolution would be referred to the Justice Department for potential prosecution and thus would go nowhere. But there is a five-year statute of limitations, and prosecutions would still be potentially viable if there is a Democratic administration after 2028. That’s also true for any potential charges for witnesses who lie before Congress or obstruct an investigation.

Of course, an ordinary mob boss doesn’t have the pardon power. Trump’s ability to pardon the malefactors who surround him will loom over this process. But pardons do not excuse a witness from testifying before Congress. Indeed, a preemptive pardon could make it more challenging for a witness to invoke the Fifth Amendment, because he or she will no longer have a well-founded fear of prosecution.

*[[Read: Trump can prosecute anyone now](https://www.theatlantic.com/politics/2026/01/trump-justice/685684/?utm_source=feed)]*

Pardons also don’t shield a witness from public shame. They don’t foreclose potential civil liability or other business or professional consequences. And a pardon can’t stop Congress from impeaching and removing a Cabinet member or other presidential appointee.

In addition, at least some witnesses will have to make a difficult calculation: *Am I really willing to commit (further) crimes and stake my liberty on the promise of a pardon from an erratic and unfocused president?* Who would want to take that bet?

In this particular investigation, the don himself will likely remain out of reach—at least where criminal liability is concerned. Given the Supreme Court’s decision on presidential immunity, even if investigations uncover criminal conduct by Trump, prosecuting that conduct after he leaves office is likely to be a nonstarter. And although the validity of such a move is untested, he’ll probably pardon himself on the way out the door as additional insurance. But Congress can ensure that he does not escape the judgment of history.

This historic election is a mandate for Congress to lead a similarly historic public reckoning. It must vigorously investigate the corruption and misconduct of the past two years. Not because those investigations will lead to criminal prosecutions. Not because the mission is to “get” Trump. But because Congress has an obligation to build a historical record of what has happened, hold those involved publicly accountable, and enact legislation designed to ensure that it can’t happen again.

items.articleBody:
**Parken statt Kabelstecken: Eine neue Funktechnik könnte E-Autos künftig helfen, die richtige Position über einer induktiven Ladestation zu finden. Im Labor bestimmte das System die Lage einer Ladespule bei einem verkleinerten Fahrzeugmodell mit einem medianen Fehler von nur 2,32 Millimetern. Ob diese Präzision auch mit echten Autos und während des Ladevorgangs gelingt, ist noch offen.**

**Suita (Japan).** Kabelloses Laden von Elektroautos funktioniert nach dem Prinzip der magnetischen Induktion: Eine Spule im Boden überträgt Energie auf eine Empfangsspule unter dem Fahrzeug. Schon wenige Zentimeter seitlicher Versatz oder eine verdrehte Stellung können die magnetische Kopplung verschlechtern und die mögliche Ladeleistung verringern.

Damit ein Elektroauto beim Parken genau über dem Ladepad zum Stehen kommt, muss es nicht nur den Stellplatz finden, sondern auch seine Position und Ausrichtung unmittelbar vor dem Halt kennen. Kameras können die flache Bodenstation bei Dunkelheit, Schmutz oder unter der Karosserie aus dem Blick verlieren, während magnetische Ortungsverfahren oft erst in unmittelbarer Nähe der Ladespule aussagekräftig sind.

### Funklaufzeit liefert den groben Kurs

Forscher der Universität Osaka (UOsaka) um Ryotaro Hada haben dafür ein Ortungsverfahren mit Ultrabreitband-Funk (UWB) entwickelt. Vier synchronisierte Funkmodule umgeben die Empfangsspule am Fahrzeug, während eine Einheit mit vier Antennenelementen an der Bodenplatte als Bezugspunkt dient.

Zunächst misst das System die Laufzeit der Funksignale zwischen den Komponenten und grenzt damit die ungefähre Position ein. Anschließend vergleicht ein Rechenverfahren die Phasen der empfangenen Funkwellen, um den seitlichen Versatz und die Drehung des Fahrzeugs genauer zu bestimmen.

Weil Antennen, Kabel und benachbarte Bauteile die Funksignale je nach Abstand und Richtung beeinflussen, muss die Anlage zuvor vermessen und kalibriert werden. Ein sogenannter Partikelfilter verfeinert anschließend die Positionsschätzung, wobei die vier Fahrzeugmodule als eine starre Anordnung ausgewertet werden. An der Entwicklung war auch der japanische Automobilzulieferer Tokai Rika beteiligt.

### Millimeterfehler am festen Haltepunkt

In einem Labortest bewegte sich ein verkleinertes Fahrzeugmodell unter Anleitung einer Bedienperson auf eine Ladeplatte zu. Die eigentliche Genauigkeitsprüfung erfolgte erst nach dem Anhalten: 200 aufeinanderfolgende UWB-Messungen an derselben festen Endposition wurden mit einer mechanisch vermessenen Referenz verglichen.

Mit Kalibrierung lag der Median des seitlichen Ortungsfehlers bei 2,32 Millimetern, der Median des Richtungsfehlers bei 0,25 Grad. Bei 90 Prozent der Messungen betrugen die Fehler höchstens 4,23 Millimeter beziehungsweise 0,72 Grad. Die Werte beschreiben damit die Präzision der Positionsschätzung im Stillstand, nicht die Abweichung eines selbstständig eingeparkten Autos.

Entscheidend war der Ausgleich systematischer Funkverzerrungen: Ohne die Korrektur winkelabhängiger Phasenfehler stieg der mediane Positionsfehler von 2,32 auf 11,93 Millimeter. In Simulationen über viele verschiedene Positionen lag der Median des Positionsfehlers bei 10,97 Millimetern und der Wert für 90 Prozent der Fälle bei 43,46 Millimetern. Der besonders geringe Fehler des stationären Modellversuchs lässt sich deshalb nicht pauschal auf alle Parkpositionen übertragen.

### Noch kein autonomer Ladevorgang

Die Rechenzeit für eine simulierte Positionsbestimmung lag im Median bei rund 13 Millisekunden, allerdings auf einem leistungsfähigen Desktopcomputer und ohne die Zeit für Funkübertragung oder Fahrzeugsteuerung. Beim praktischen Vorführen lenkte eine Bedienperson das Modell anhand der angezeigten Positionsdaten. Ein automatisch geregeltes Einparken oder Laden wurde nicht erprobt.

Noch steht damit nur fest, dass die kalibrierte Funkanlage ihre relative Position in einem kontrollierten Modellaufbau sehr genau schätzen kann. Ob das auch mit einem vollständigen Fahrzeug, dessen Metallunterboden und wechselnden Umgebungsbedingungen funktioniert, ist nicht nachgewiesen.

> „Eine Rechenmethode in ein funktionierendes System umzusetzen, erforderte beträchtliches Ausprobieren. Wir hoffen, dass diese Forschung zu einer Zukunft beiträgt, in der Elektroautos einfach durch Parken geladen werden, ähnlich wie Smartphones auf kabellosen Ladegeräten“, sagt Ryotaro Hada.

Vor einem praktischen Einsatz sind Tests mit Fahrzeugen in Originalgröße, im Freien und bei tatsächlich eingeschalteter Energieübertragung erforderlich. Außerdem muss sich zeigen, wie stabil die Kalibrierung bei Temperaturwechseln, veränderter Fahrzeughöhe und störenden Funkreflexionen bleibt. Erst dann lässt sich beurteilen, ob die millimetergenaue Ortung auch den Ladealltag erleichtern kann.

Quellen:

- Originalstudie im Fachmagazin [IEEE Open Journal of Vehicular Technology](https://doi.org/10.1109/OJVT.2026.3725689), doi: 10.1109/OJVT.2026.3725689
- Offizielle Studienmitteilung von [The University of Osaka](https://www.asiaresearchnews.com/content/radio-waves-pave-way-effortless-ev-charging) (UOsaka)

items.articleBody:
**by David Hoyt**

Edith Farnsworth House on the Fox River near Plano, Illinois. (Source: Edith Fansworth Papers, [Internet Archives](https://archive.org/details/mms_farnsworth/page/n138/mode/thumb)).

About an hour’s drive southwest of Chicago is a grassy bank on the shore of the Fox River where, according to some, the predominant architecture of the twentieth century first took shape. It was here that a precocious and independent-minded physician, Edith Farnsworth, asked her newly-emigrated German friend and paramour, Mies van der Rohe, to build her a country cottage. He did so, after a fashion.

The structure known as Farnsworth House stands outside of the village of Plano, Illinois. It was begun in 1945 and completed in 1951. By the time it was “move-in ready”, its new owner declared it unlivable, and broke off relations with the architect, at which point Mies filed a lien against her and Farnsworth responded with a countersuit against the patron saint of modernism.

A sculptural masterpiece of steel frame construction, the house seems to float above the meadow as if defying gravity, wrapped in glass without internal partition as if to announce to obsolescence of privacy well before the advent of social media. Yet it was too hot in summer, and frigid in winter. It lacked adequate ventilation, was prone to leaks from the roof and window frames, and was located squarely within the flood plain of the Fox River, which has inundated it several times.

Farnsworth’s disappointment with the structure was given metaphorical expression in an unpublished poem she wrote in 1960. Yet the poem, titled “Artifact,” is more than a metaphor. It announces a fundamental flaw in the paradigm of glass-and-steel modernism that has come to dominate so much of our built environment. The large expanses of sheet glass that seemed to “let the outside in” (as Mies put it) actually did the opposite: they gave an illusion of intimacy with nature while walling it off. The price paid for this illusion, among other costs, was the ongoing destruction of wild and free-flying birds crashing into it.

The poem reads in full:

> Artifact.
> The dawn was close this morning when I woke
> To hear some flying creatures strike the pane
> Of glass beside my bed – strike and flutter
> For a moment, strike and beat
> Bewildered wings upon the glass.
> There was no light.
> It was not day, or night.
> I could not see the wounded flying thing
> But I could hear the fluttering, breaking wing
> Beating its moment out upon my pane
> Of glass. Why does it not recoil, or die?
> The unseen wings are slipping down the pane;
> The splintered feathers agonize in vain.
> The moments pass
> And in the grass
> Below, there lies
> My hope, and dies
> (Source: Edith Farnsworth Papers, Newberry Library Archives)

Elements of Farnsworth House – the low-rising staircase, the exposed H-beams – would show up in later works such as the Illinois Institute of Technology campus, the twin residential high-rises at 860/880 Lake Shore Drive, and elsewhere. Scholars have duly traced these genealogies of style. But they have mostly overlooked what Edith Farnsworth experienced in the predawn hours of a morning in 1961, and what most people have at some point likely experienced in their own home. Wherever buildings with large expanses of glass are built, be they multi-story curtain walls or living room picture windows, birds collide with them, most often fatally.

The biggest bird killer in Toronto, on the shore of Lake Ontario and thus a major migratory stopover, is the Toronto Dominion Center (1967), designed by Mies van der Rohe. The largest avian mortality event known in Chicago, and one of the most severe ever recorded in the United States, and perhaps anywhere, occurred over the night of October 4-5, 2023, when nearly 1,000 birds died in collisions with the giant glass walls of a single building: McCormick Place (1971). The building was designed by two students and former employees of Mies van der Rohe.

A sample of the 1,000 migratory birds killed in collision with McCormick Place’s glass walls on the single night of October 4-5, 2023. ([Lauren Nassef/Chicago Field Museum via AP](https://www.npr.org/2023/10/09/1204641722/nearly-1-000-migrating-birds-died-after-crashing-into-chicago-building))

In roughly the same way that modernist art critics such as Clement Greenberg, roughly contemporary with Mies, (1909-1994) theorized the trend towards painterly abstraction as an expansion of the subject beyond the frame containing it, the predominance of glass in modern architecture is envisioned as a way of making a building transparent, of exceeding its structure, of making its own steel frame disappear. It is a way of removing itself from any context, of “letting the outside in” – without, on the other hand, providing any real connection to it.

The American architect and broker of German modernism in the United States, Philip Johnson, recognized that the new architecture was, from a visual and external point of view, all about larger glass surface area. (Johnson’s own Wells Fargo Center (1983) in downtown Denver, Colorado, has been marked as the deadliest building for migratory birds in that city).

This trend began in the downtown Chicago of the 1880s, as engineering advances facilitated the construction of multi-story consumer emporia and allowed for the larger windows which delighted shoppers and filled terra cotta-clad buildings with natural light. Johnson sees this tendency of modernism as, coining a matchless phrase, one of “maximal fenestration.” “Windows constitute a more important element in modern architecture than they have in any architecture since that of the Gothic cathedrals,” wrote Johnson in his paradigmatic 1931 handbook, *The International Style*.

Mies grew up in the shadow of one such cathedral, commissioned by the Emperor of the Franks, Charlemagne, at Aachen. One of the oldest and greatest cathedrals in Europe, it is known as the *Glashaus* for its palpable yearning to break free from masonry constraints so that its windows can harvest their light from the heavens. The years of Mies’ early adulthood in the post-war Weimar Republic were the seedbed for countless utopian dreams and projects, including one movement which sought to design future buildings of the German republic from colored crystals, a sort of secularization of the Gothic stained-glass window, but with a shared intention of elevating the soul.

Two of Mies’ earliest drawings from this period, representing a transition from expressionist fantasy to Bauhaus functionality, and considered by scholars as among the greatest buildings never built, are a pair of glass-walled skyscrapers situated in Berlin.

Mies van der Rohe’s 1921 skyscraper designs for the Friedrichstrasse, Berlin. (Source: [MOMA](https://www.moma.org/collection/works/787))

This mystical aspiration for light and invisibility in architecture dates to the emergence of German modernism in the immediate aftermath of World War One, but continues today in the market for ever taller condo towers with ever better views. What emerged as a functional element in the service of social liberation and transparency in the 1920’s is now a commodity allowing for aesthetic consumption from atop supertall condo towers or unobstructed lake house panoramas.

Absent mindful adaptation, both kill birds in great numbers.

As one trade website remarks, in “[A Trend in Modern Architecture: More Glass](https://www.stainless-structurals.com/blog/a-trend-in-modern-architecture-more-glass/),”

> One walk around New York City, Chicago, Los Angeles or Seattle and one can see the … trend of larger curtain walls, including those with glass to make the building envelope seem almost transparent … Floor to ceiling glass spans are growing by the day as architects want sustainable designs with breathtaking views.

While there are voices within the architectural establishment that have begun to question Johnson’s drive for maximal fenestration, in the typical list of problems cited, bird mortality is almost never mentioned. The issues are more often of the LEED-sustainability sort, centered on metrics of consumption, rather than an ecological framework centered on organic relations. One spectacular example of this is the sparkling new BMO Tower at 320 South Canal (2022). Located on the banks of the Chicago River in what has become a canyon of glass-walled skyscrapers, it is a documented bird-killer. It is also a LEED Gold-certified building pitching itself as “Chicago’s Healthiest Office Tower.”

A Common Yellowthroat, victim of collision with BMO Tower at 320 S. Canal on October 5, 2022. ([Robyn Detterline, Chicago Ornithological Society](https://www.chicagobirder.org/blog/2023/10/12/chicagos-bird-friendly-design-ordinance-where-things-stand))

Certain architects are concerned with climate change, resource consumption, or that catch-all category of neoliberal virtue, energy efficiency. Industry correspondingly provides solutions in the form of glass with better thermal regulation (“modulating capacity”), panels that contain or serve as photovoltaic cells, or “cold bending” glass that can be shaped one way and then reused in another. The adoption of architectural glass with simple and cheap accommodations for wildlife seems to be a derogation in a primarily anthropocentric world of designing and raising buildings.

An inspiring but limited exception to this is state of affairs can be seen in the work of architect Jeanne Gang, founder of the Studio Gang firm headquartered in Chicago and a sponsor of the exhibit [Flyway City: Architecture for a Flourishing Ecosystem](https://www.architecture.org/visit-the-center/exhibitions/flyway-city), currently running at the Chicago Architecture Center. Gang is perhaps best known for her decision, like Wright a century before, to ‘break the box’ – the ‘box’ for Gang being the steel-glass cage of modernism, rather than the dim cubbyholes of the Victorian interior in Wright’s time. The style is exemplified in her 2009 Chicago River tower, ‘Aqua’. Popularly appreciated for its apparent vertical curvature, suggestive of the nearby lakeshore on a summer day, it is in fact intentionally bird-friendly. Specifications called for fritted glass throughout, which make windows visible to birds, and undulating balcony platforms, which interrupt reflections confusing to birds.

Demonstration bird-friendly window-treatments. Chicago Architecture Center’s [Flyway City](https://www.architecture.org/visit-the-center/exhibitions/flyway-city) Exhibit, October 2026.

The exhibit serves a much needed educational purpose, for the public remains largely ignorant of avian window strikes and their appalling death toll. Partly this is because building managers and advocacy groups alike both descend on downtown pavements before the first light of dawn to gather carcasses and send any survivors to a suburban forest preserve hospital specializing in wildlife rehabilitation. The public thus rarely encounters the physical results of avian window strikes. *Flyway City* presents one – very small – display case with half a dozen ‘skins’, or preserved bird carcasses, recovered from various addresses in the Loop, together with a poignant [documentary short](https://vimeo.com/1200153342) which features a young volunteer witnessing the mortal collision in real time of a bird (what appears to be a Dark-eyed junco) and an all-glass tower along the Chicago River. The film may be the most compelling feature of the exhibition.

The address in question, in case you are curious, is [155 North Wacker](https://www.gpchicago.com/architecture/155-north-wacker/).

Studio Gang is but one firm facing down a very, very large problem, led by a principal who is a strong advocate of bird-friendly design. But even this firm has recently built a very tall, all-glass tower (the [St. Regis](https://studiogang.com/projects/vista-tower/), 2021) that now commands its section of lakefront flyway. The building deploys several collision-deterring elements, but not the gold standard of fritted or patterned glass, widely understood to be the most effective means of steering birds away from windows. I am unable to find any information – which is typically guarded, both by property owners and by volunteer collision monitors – as to how many birds strike the St. Regis.

But the larger point is that, as Jeanne Gang openly calls for, and as *Flyway City* openly advocates, municipal regulations are necessary to reduce Chicago’s architectural carnage. Self-policing of architectural firms and the developers who realize their designs is no more reliable than it is with industrial pollution, banking, or artificial intelligence. This is why a movement has arisen for the passage of a municipal, bird-friendly building ordinance to mandate certain safety elements in all new construction.

Predictably, the ordinance runs into opposition in City Council from alderpersons representing major property management firms and architectural designers in downtown Chicago. First introduced in 2019, it has languished for nigh on a decade with no prospect of passage in sight. The chief objection, also predictable, is to allegedly higher construction costs and the follow-on effects that this presumably leads to, like fewer jobs. This hasn’t prevented architecturally and geographically comparable cities such as New York or San Francisco from passing mandatory bird safety ordinances. Though one need not look so far afield for exemplars: already in Chicago’s near-north suburbs of Evanston and Skokie, bird-friendly building ordinances have passed; and since it was signed into law by Governor J.B. Pritzker in 2021, the State of Illinois mandates all state-owned buildings must use patterned glass on 90% of glass exteriors to forty feet in elevation.

The absence of a mandatory bird-safe building ordinance in Chicago has resulted in a decade of heedless, see-through pleasure boxes rising along the River and elsewhere, such as Norman Foster’s Michigan Avenue [Apple Store](https://www.architecture.org/online-resources/buildings-of-chicago/apple-michigan-avenue) (celebrated in [Architectural Digest](https://www.architecturaldigest.com/story/apple-store-norman-foster-chicago-waterfront)), 150 North [Riverside Plaza](https://www.architecture.org/online-resources/buildings-of-chicago/150-north-riverside), and the shamelessly obtuse [Salesforce Tower](https://www.333wolfpoint.com/) on the Chicago River. Typically, buildings such as these are conceived with no bird-friendly accommodations, as if those involved were still living in a 1920’s Bauhaus bubble and were too busy to read the headlines about cratering North American bird populations. Though some developer/owners may take action after the fact to address collisions, as happened after much public shaming at McCormick Place and the Apple Store, or offer bird-friendly assurances before building, as at the riverfront Bally’s Casino, there is no guarantee that whatever measures are taken will sufficient to address the problem in the absence of legal requirement.

Rendering of approved Bally’s Casino on file with the [Chicago Department of Planning](https://www.chicago.gov/city/en/sites/chicago-casino/home/permanent-casino/renderings.html).

Opponents of a city bird-friendly building ordinance argue that it would be costly, cumbersome to administer, and stifling of housing supply. The leading researcher on avian window strikes in North America, [Daniel Klem](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/396092634_Bird-window_collisions_a_critical_review), argues in a 2025 paper that a municipal law would have the effect of driving up demand for patterned glass, which in turn would eventually drive down costs, as has happened in the market for photovoltaics – at which point, compliance becomes less painful for developers.

Klem also points out that specifying treated glass in construction designs typically accounts for less than one percent of total project costs, and even less when average cost overruns are included. And, as an urban planner told me recently, glass is actually the cheapest cladding for a building. It costs much more to clad a structure in marble or Indiana limestone, both of which are comparable to modern glass in terms of thermal efficiency. The extreme bottom-line mentality evident here will never satisfactorily address the problem of its own accord. This is why the public must be rallied to the cause. But before that can happen, the public must be educated. And, as I discover every day, the majority of people are simply unaware of the problem and its proportions: according to the latest research, between 1.28 billion to over 3.46 billion birds die from window collisions each year in North America alone.

One thing that can quickly awaken public opinion is publicity stemming from a mass mortality event such as occurred at McCormick Place in 2023. For decades, birders and ornithologists lodged complaints with the massive state-run facility on the shore of Lake Michigan, and a total of over 40,000 dead birds had been gathered there since its initial construction. It was only after the shocking overnight mortality event of October 4-5 that public sentiment became too strong and widespread for McCormick Place to resist change any longer. Over the course of three months in the following summer of 2024, the facility applied collision deterrent film to all of its exterior glass, at a cost of $1.2 million. A very similar chain of events unfolded in Toronto around the Dominion Center Building in 2021.

Glass addiction: Chicago’s Salesforce Tower (2023)

Anyone contemplating the work of Chicago’s Louis Sullivan can’t help but be absorbed by the delicate and encompassing vegetal patterns that seem to grow like vines and branches directly out of stone or metal, echoing French *art nouveau* but from a distinctly American point of origin. This progenitor of the prairie school sought to assimilate the built to the organic and to the simple forms and materials of the Midwestern landscape. The modernism of Mies van der Rohe, on the other hand, was born from the social strife and class conflict of Central Europe, and was welded to an aesthetic of the Machine. Forms of ornamentation – themselves anathema in the heated politics of central European artistic modernism – evolved to suit the local settings in which Sullivan and Wright worked, meant to echo the particularity of place, much the way Fernand Braudel lovingly catalogued the various forms of rooftops across provincial France. For Mies and Johnson and the practitioners of the International Style who came after them, all of this echoing and mimicking and organicism was replaced by glass. Glass does not relate to or echo a place. It allows you to *look* *at* a place, from noplace in particular.

Unless you happen to be a bird, in which case, glass is what you never see before it kills you.

items.articleBody:
In the fall of 2016, Yang Licai traveled to the States from China and spent a few months in our home in West Texas while we were away for work. It was there that he finished [Pee Poems](https://circumferencebooks.com/book/pee-poems-second-edition). The train that tries to wake him again and again in these poems is the same train that succeeds in waking us each morning, and perhaps this serves as a metaphor for the biggest challenge we faced as translators of this book: how to bring forth the wonderful spirit of its author, who chooses the difficult dream over an easy life.

We became friends with Yang in 2012, when we all lived at Akademie Schloss Solitude, an artist residency in Germany. He was there as a music/sound fellow, but beyond his performances and various other creative practices, he is known as a gardener, builder, teacher, and promoter of experimental music. For many years Yang Licai ran an art space and music store in the 798 district in Beijing, and in fact we first crossed paths with him there, very briefly, in 2009. By that time, financial and political forces had pushed out nearly all the other artist-run spaces, so his tiny store, with a wall of floor-to-ceiling CDs, was particularly memorable. We both recollect him calling out a greeting from the loft above. Within a year, authorities would ransack this space and violently force him out.

In an interview conducted during the protest he staged immediately after the destruction of his store and home, Lao Yang stated: “This is not performance art. Art is like a lame act of charity in the face of life’s cruelty. When someone sets himself ablaze with gasoline, just to illuminate his sabotaged home, it naturally eclipses the impact of any work of art.... Until we have secured our rights, we cannot practice art, cannot live with art, cannot think artistically or observe this world with an artistic eye.” Years later he explained his own creative practice to us in this context, saying that it is not art, but what comes before, when art is not possible. “Don’t call me a poet, call me a piss person,” he writes at the beginning of this collection.

Yang has also called himself a “noise maker and its noise.” From his writing it is clear that the clamor he makes is directed beyond the ear, to the social and spiritual origins of the listener’s attention. One of our easier tasks was conveying the urgency of *Pee Poems*, but what proved much more difficult was rendering the mix of subtlety and straightforwardness in his language. In his Chinese text, there is often an orthographic interrogation of characters. Take for example the aphoristic fragment “人 从 众 / 众 从 人” (literally: “person from multitude / multitude from person”), which simply shows us the movement from the pictograph for “person” (人) to the compound ideographs “from” (从) and “multitude” (众). This is a particularly beautiful palindrome in which the movement from person to multitude is mirrored, to show both creation and decreation; or, there is a contract in the language itself (the formation of the characters) between the singular and the plural, which the author is helping us remember. The multitude is built from the person, and that conjunction itself—from—requires a movement from one (person) to two. Our thoughts went first to the seventh section of George Oppen’s “Of Being Numerous” (“Obsessed, bewildered // By the shipwreck / Of the singular // We have chosen the meaning / Of being numerous.”), but this and other references would be politically misleading, so in the end we decided to make the simplest translation we could think of: “One of many / many of one.”

Language play and puns are frequently used in *Pee Poems*, and readers of our English translation might think of this book in conversation with works by Marcel Duchamp and [John Cage](https://tricycle.org/magazine/taking-chances/). Seeing as Yang Licai was one of the early apostles of sound art and experimental music in China in the 2000s, these readers would not be wrong—one can imagine him nodding in agreement to Cage’s “Farting, don’t think, just fart,” or Duchamp’s “Art is not about itself but the attention we bring to it.” Or one might think of the Black Mountain poets or the anti-poems of Nicanor Parra. But focusing on Western aesthetics obscures this young Chinese poet’s radicality, as well as his place in traditions that go back many hundreds of years. In the style of some Tang dynasty poets, Yang Licai writes intensely about solitude, longing, and friendship, but like Zhuangzi, he is concerned primarily with the most complex and elusive of concepts: freedom and peace. Having a creative practice that actively promotes these ideas and denounces their antagonists, Yang lives with risks that most of us can’t imagine.

Tied closely to these themes of freedom and attention is Yang Licai’s spiritual inquiry, which recalls Chan and Zen thinkers like Shiwu, [Hanshan](https://tricycle.org/article/hanshan-and-shide/), [Dogen](https://tricycle.org/author/eiheidogenzenji/), and [Ryokan](https://tricycle.org/article/ryokan-poems/). The association is made explicit in Yang’s short piece “Poetry,” in which he takes apart the title character, *shi* (詩). The constituent parts, or radicals, are thus made to speak for themselves: “言寸土 / 言寺” (“Shallow-dirt speak / Temple speak”). As Red Pine points out in the preface to his wonderful translation of *Poems of the Masters*, the second part (寺) of the word for poetry (詩) was originally written *zhi* (詩), “meaning ‘from the heart,’ and the later form was simply the result of calligraphic shorthand and subsequent convention. Hence the word for poetry does not mean ‘language of the court/temple’ but the ‘language of the heart.’ ”

In working together to translate this book by our friend, we were constantly reminded of Yang’s great kindness, humor, and intelligence. We thought back on conversations about philosophy, plants, food, travel, love, and so much more, and we reminisced about his unique combination of fierceness and grace. Over the years, Yang Licai’s bravery and integrity have inspired us to examine our own beliefs and choices, so it’s been a distinct pleasure to discuss and think about his writing. In a speech translated by Rosmarie Waldrop, Paul Celan said that “a poem, being an instance of language, hence essentially dialogue, may be a letter in a bottle thrown out to sea with the—surely not always strong—hope that it may somehow wash up somewhere, perhaps on a shoreline of the heart.” The act of translation may be an answer to and an echo of that hope, and we thank you for reading our version of Yang Licai’s *Pee Poems*.

*–Joshua Edwards & Lynn Xu*

## Midnight Train Love Letter (Part I)

The potato flings farmer into field

The stone tosses the primordial into time

The planet hides galaxies in nebulae

Eyes are led by the gaze into love

O!

Great compassionate Buddha

Buddha who has long been compassionate My dearest

Look at that

How can I show you my heart

Having lost my footing in the water

Step by lotus-flower step

## Midnight Train Love Letter (Part II)

If night is gentle

Evil will fall away

In succession the landscape turns

The singing voice that steel unfolds

This restless journey continues

And my heart is filled with tenderness

For you, spirited and vivacious

And for the souls of the lonely multitude

For this world bright with evil

And for our love, I can turn away from it all

Except there’s not simply gentleness

And yet there is a means to be at peace

With the suffering of sentient beings

And the discord of the mundane world

I experience this moment quietly

Heart like a lotus flower

## Second Morning in West Texas

The train left my childhood

Not knowing its destination

Hometown at my back

I try to catch up, running barefoot

Thirty years west of the river

Thirty years east of the river

In Marfa

The train tries to wake me again and again

But my dreams, not yet over,

Are determined to last until morning

The train carries away dream and hometown

Morning and I

Remain in Marfa

I’m that anxious farmer

Seeds in hand

Ceaselessly walking barefoot

Searching all over for land

He says

The ruins are solemn and endless

Buddha is without limits

Civilization and its funerals

I have no choice but to sow seeds in rubble

He says

Greet the sightless to see

Let the deaf hear

Wait for the silent to speak

When twilight is nigh

I’m going to lose him

You’re going to lose me

We’re going to lose everything

♦

*These selections are from* [Pee Poems](https://circumferencebooks.com/book/pee-poems-second-edition) *, which is available from Circumference Books. Reprinted with permission from the authors and publisher.*

Improving on a timeless recipe

@media screen and (max-width: 767px) {
}

The bezier curve is a staple of CAD and computer graphics. Like Bic pens, the design is decades old and they're everywhere. You'll often find them as the default or only choice in various illustration and animation tools.

Conceived by Paul de Casteljau in 1959, and refined by Pierre Bézier in the 1960s at Renault, the enduring appeal of the bezier curve lies in its simplicity. While more sophisticated curves have been invented, and
new ones continue to be proposed, these are limited to specific domains, like high-precision CAD or road design. In general use, the bezier stubbornly refuses to be dethroned, despite its shortcomings.

Hence bezier curves are a piece of legacy tech we appear to be stuck with. As a software engineer, my question then is: can we make beziers better without invalidating all the tech built on and with them?

The answer is yes.

Source

Lerp-a-derp

Drawing a bezier curve is a surprisingly simple and linear process:

Tip: All the diagrams in this post are fully interactive.

Given a series of control points, we connect them with lines. We then run along those lines simultaneously, to produce new points, which can be connected again. This process is repeated until we are left with a single point, which lies on the curve.

This construction makes beziers far more regular than they might first appear.

The linear interpolations (aka lerps) can be summarized into a single compact formula, e.g. for 4 control points $ \left(A, B, C, D\right) $:

$$ \gamma \left( t \right) = A \cdot \left(1 - t\right)^3 + B \cdot 3 \left(1 - t\right)^2 t + C \cdot 3 \left(1 - t\right) t^2 + D \cdot t^3 $$

The rule is simple: descending powers of $\left(1 - t\right)$, ascending powers of $t$, with coefficients taken from the n'th row of Pascal's triangle:

$$
\begin{array}{ccccccccccccc}
&&&&&& 1 \\
&&&&& 1 && 1 \\
&&&& 1 && 2 && 1 \\
&&& 1 && 3 && 3 && 1 \\
&& 1 && 4 && 6 && 4 && 1 \\
&1 && 5 && 10 && 10 && 5 && 1 \\
... &&&&&& ... &&&&&& ... \\
\end{array}
$$

For curves in 2D and 3D, the formula is applied to the individual X, Y or Z coordinates.

While beziers can be constructed for any number of control points, the common practice is to only use cubic beziers with 4 control points. This is because the curve is only guaranteed to cross through the first and last control point, which makes higher degree beziers more difficult to shape.

Larger curves are instead constructed by joining together multiple cubic bezier segments, with the tangents lined up to create a segmented curve that appears smooth:

This is the cubic bezier spline, as commonly understood. The precision "pen tool" in most drawing apps then consists of drawing and editing the control points, rather than drawing curves directly.

A Lie Told Everywhere

Pen tools typically have a few different modes for the control points:

Intuitively these represent various degrees of smoothness. Symmetric tangents are offered as the smoothest option, with some qualities of smoothness being lost as you relax the constraints.

In reality this is completely wrong, and this is easy to demonstrate.

Bezier curves can be split exactly, by reading off the new control points from the interpolation diagram:

The left and right segments are 100% identical to the original curve, and always join up perfectly at the seam. Yet the tangents in the middle will be asymmetric except for one split near the middle. This can be confirmed using a curvature comb which represents the (inverse) radius of curvature at every point:

The curvature comb remains continuous, with no jumps.

This means that whether or not adjacent tangents are of equal length, i.e. symmetric, is completely irrelevant. Attempting to draw smooth and intuitive bezier curves this way is a fool's errand.

A simple way to improve this is to treat the tangents as relative rather than absolute. e.g. We can make them proportional to the distance between the start and end of each segment:

This spline is easier to edit, because as you move each curve point around, the adjacent segments naturally flex to get out of the way. There are far fewer cusps created this way. Editing the tangents remains the same.

However if we plot curvature again, we can tell this isn't a great solution:

Scaling tangents proportionally doesn't guarantee that curvature is preserved as you edit, nor does curvature remain continuous from one segment to the next.

This also shows that offering users a curvature comb visualization as a "helpful tool" is really quite mean: adjusting the curvature on one end will also affect the other side, requiring repeated adjustments back and forth until it's close enough.

Handle Carefully

A much more effective strategy is to work with curvature directly.

While this is a difficult problem in general, it turns out there are some surprising relationships here, which we can observe directly:

Consider the curvature at the start of segment $A-B-C-D$. This is affected only by the positions of $A$, $B$ and $C$. Point $D$ can be moved freely if it's detached from $C$.

Furthermore, because the tangent $A-B$ is horizontal, only the vertical position of $C$ matters. This is a result of the underlying linear interpolations, which end up cancelling out a lot of terms in the formulas.

The curvature at $A$ is therefor only affected by the length of $A-B$, and the perpendicular distance from $C$ to $A-B$. The same applies to $D$ on the other side with $C-D$ and $B$.

This isn't very useful by itself though. When we move a curve point ($A$ or $D$), typically the adjacent control point ($B$ or $C$) is moved as well to preserve the tangent. And when we turn a symmetric or asymmetric tangent, the adjacent tangent in the next segment is turned by the same angle, altering the curvature on that side.

Still, this shows that preserving curvature is not by itself a crazy idea and can be done simply by scaling the tangents appropriately. The rules would be simple:

When we move a curve point, we have to preserve the start and end curvature in the adjacent segments

When we move a tangent, we have to preserve the curvature on the opposite end of the current segment, as well as on both sides of the adjacent segment

This ought to produce an editing experience where the curve actually respects your intent. Except not quite:

Moving curve points works great, but when turning a tangent, the length of that tangent is itself a poor representation of the user's intent. Small changes can cause huge shifts in curvature, which can cause the curve to jump around and explode unexpectedly as it tries to find a matching solution.

Hence it's better to work with curvature handles instead, where the length corresponds directly to curvature:

Unlike the curvature comb, the length of the handles is the non-inverted radius of curvature, which is the more natural choice.

These handles are very stable and can be converted just-in-time to classic bezier control points, without needing to round-trip back and forth between the two representations. Helpfully, this also avoids numerical drift.

Goldilocks

To actually pull this off, we need to solve for the lengths $l_0$ and $l_1$ of the tangents, given the desired curvatures $k_0$ and $k_1$, the start/end points $A$ and $D$, and the unit-length tangents at the start/end.

Given a curve $\gamma\left(t\right)$, we can express the unit tangent vector $\mathbf{T}\left(t\right)$ as the normalized derivative:

$$ \mathbf{T}\left(t\right) = \frac{\displaystyle \gamma'\left(t\right)}{\displaystyle |γ'\left(t\right)|} $$

This can be used to find the curvature vector $\mathbf{K}\left(t\right)$ via two vector cross products using the first and second derivative:

$$ \mathbf{K}\left(t\right) = \mathbf{T}\left(t\right) \times \frac{\gamma''\left(t\right)}{|\gamma'\left(t\right)|^2} \times \mathbf{T}\left(t\right) $$

The cross products ensure that $\mathbf{K}\left(t\right)$ is perpendicular to $\mathbf{T}\left(t\right)$, i.e. they extract the normal vector component of the middle term. Now we can solve for $\mathbf{K}\left(0\right) = k_0$ and $\mathbf{K}\left(1\right) = k_1$.

After working through the math, we end up with a quadratic system of equations in $l_0$ and $l_1$:

$$
\begin{cases}
a_0 \cdot l_0^2 + b \cdot l_1 + c_0 = 0 \\[0.3em]
a_1 \cdot l_1^2 + b \cdot l_0 + c_1 = 0
\end{cases}
$$

Where:

$$
\begin{array}{lcl}
a_0 & = & ±|k_0| \\[0.3em]
a_1 & = & ±|k_1| \\[0.3em]
b & = & 2 \cdot |\mathbf{T}(0) \times \mathbf{T}(1)| \\[0.3em]
c_0 & = & 6 \cdot |\mathbf{T}(0) \times (D - A)| \\[0.3em]
c_1 & = & 6 \cdot |\mathbf{T}(1) \times (A - D)| \\[0.3em]
\end{array}
$$

This captures a few things:

The sign of the curvature $k_i$ defines whether the curve turns clockwise or counterclockwise. When moving curve points around, the curve may be forced to flip, hence the $±$ is necessary, and both signs can change independently.

The coupling between $l_0$ and $l_1$ is influenced only by $b$. If $b = 0$, then the two equations are independent and the problem is trivial to solve. This corresponds to the situation where the two tangents are parallel.

The constant term $c_i$ is influenced only by the perpendicular distance $D - A$ (or $A - D$) to the tangent $\mathbf{T_i}$. This matches the earlier finding that only perpendicular distance affects curvature.

Hence, the problem is reduced to finding the intersection of two double-parabolas, one horizontal and one vertical:

The two sides of each double-parabola represent bending clockwise or counterclockwise. We have to solve 4 times, one for each sign combination $\left(+,+\right)$, $\left(+,-\right)$, $\left(-,+\right)$, $\left(-,-\right)$.

To solve this system, we can rewrite either of the equations to isolate $l_1$ or $l_0$:

$$
l_1 = \frac{\displaystyle -a_0 \cdot l_0^2 - c_0}{\displaystyle b} \\[0.5em]
l_0 = \frac{\displaystyle -a_1 \cdot l_1^2 - c_1}{\displaystyle b}
$$

Pick one, and square it to plug it into the other original equation as the $l_1^2$ or $l_0^2$ term. This produces a quartic equation in the other variable (resp. $l_0$ or $l_1$), which can be solved directly using the quartic formula.

We can then compute the other $l_i$, either:

$$
l_1 = \sqrt{\frac{\displaystyle -b \cdot l_0 - c_1}{\displaystyle a_1}} \\[0.5em]
l_0 = \sqrt{\frac{\displaystyle -b \cdot l_1 - c_0}{\displaystyle a_0}}
$$

Not all solutions of the quartic will be actual solutions to the system however, because of the squaring. So we have to double check that the original equations hold before accepting a solution for $\left(l_0, l_1\right)$.

We also want to reject solutions where $l_0

For corner-type points, one or both $k_i$'s are infinite. This is straightforward to solve as the matching $l_i$ is zero and the other can be computed directly.

Grouper and Snapper

Unfortunately if there are multiple solutions, these each represent a different curve:

Having the curve jump around as you edit it would be a very bad editing experience, but there is no obvious way to pick the right one.

One strategy would be to remember the previous $l_0$ and $l_1$ as you edit, and pick the solution that is closest to the previous curve. However this would introduce path-dependence into editing, where the order and direction that you moved points around in affects which curve you end up with. For a drawing tool, this is quite frustrating and undesirable.

Different solutions to the equation can also appear and vanish suddenly, so this wouldn't eliminate popping either, merely reduce it.

Ideally the resulting curvatures should always change smoothly themselves. This can be accomplished by designing an appropriate weighting heuristic for the solutions, and calculating their weighted average.

1) The forbidden regions:

When a solution approaches either $l_0

These solutions are unstable and should be avoided. To detect this, I calculate the gradient vector of each equation.

$$
\mathbf{g_0} = \begin{bmatrix}2 \cdot a_0 \cdot l_0 & b\end{bmatrix} \\[0.3em]
\mathbf{g_1} = \begin{bmatrix}b & 2 \cdot a_1 \cdot l_1\end{bmatrix}
$$

The angle between them can be found via their dot product, after dividing by their respective lengths:

$$
\cos \theta = \frac{\displaystyle \mathbf{g_0} \cdot \mathbf{g_1}}{\displaystyle |\mathbf{g_0}||\mathbf{g_1}|}
$$

A value close to $-1$ means two opposite-bending parabolas, while a value close to $1$ means two aligned parabolas. The latter is not as bad, as this implies many almost-equivalent solutions.

3) When the radius of curvature is very big compared to the bezier itself, one of the possible solutions is for the curve to cross through itself, forming a loop. This should be discouraged:

We can divide by the length of $|\mathbf{l}|$ i.e. $\sqrt{l_0^2 + l_1^2}$, preferring solutions that have shorter tangents.

Putting it all together, the weighting heuristic I chose is:

$$
w_{heuristic}\left(\mathbf{l}\right) = \left(\frac{\displaystyle l_0 \cdot l_1 \cdot \arccos\left(-\cos \theta\right)}{\displaystyle |\mathbf{l}|^2}\right)^2
$$

Large $|\mathbf{l}|$'s represent undesirable solutions, so should be strongly penalized and only chosen if they are the only option

When the entire heuristic approaches $0$, the influence should vanish smoothly, hence the overall squaring

Using this as the weight, the resulting bezier curves always change smoothly, even when the start and end are moved around and through each other.

But when multiple solutions are averaged together, the resulting $(l_0, l_1)$ is not necessarily a solution to the original system. This means the resulting curvatures are not always exact, even when there is an exact solution nearby.

To mitigate this, we can add an additional resampling step, where we re-weigh the solutions according to the inverse distance^4 to the weighted average:

$$
w_{sample}\left(\mathbf{l}\right) = \frac{1}{|\mathbf{l} - \mathbf{l}_{average}|^4}
$$

This causes the solution to snap smoothly to exact solutions when available.

Migratory Curves

What's especially nice about this approach is that it can largely be slotted into existing systems with little modification required.

The UI of adjusting and editing bezier handles can be kept, including the notion of the 4 point types. Just the meaning of the lengths of the tangents changes. Converting an asymmetric point to a symmetric point will actually equalize the curvature of the left and right side, which is what the user actually wants.

The internal representation can mostly remain the same type, i.e. a series of points, just those points represent curvature tangents, not bezier tangents. Though it's better to explicitly store the unit length tangents and curvatures directly, which is more numerically stable. For the demos here I made pairwise conversion functions between curvature handles ↔︎ points/tangents/curvatures ↔︎ bezier handles.

Splitting a curvature bezier is a lot simpler than splitting a classic bezier, because the start and end handles don't change at all, and the newly created handles are symmetric:

There is one remaining flaw though. When splitting a curve with an S-bend, the splits near the bend are not exact:

The heuristic picks the wrong curve on one or both sides. This can be fixed by remembering the specific orientation of the curvature, and only flipping the curvature sign when necessary. Though this does introduce some minimal path-dependence into editing.

So really you would need to expose this in the UI as an extra orientation toggle for ambiguous control points. It would also mean that the internal representation has to be in tangent + signed curvature form to be fully stable, not just curvature handles.

Near the S-bend, the radius of curvature—and thus the handle size—effectively becomes infinite, because $|k|$ becomes $0$. The bezier control points lie on a straight line, as perpendicular distance to the tangent is zero.

So even when handled exactly, this can still create impractically large curvature handles. Perhaps what's needed is a 5th "Inflection" point type, for points with exactly zero $|k|$, though such points tend to be very unstable, and sometimes no solution exists:

To migrate a classic bezier to a curvature bezier, you can measure the unit tangents and curvature at the start and end. In the vast majority of cases this will result in the exact same curve. If it doesn't, then you must split the original bezier to avoid the ambiguity.

For complex operations on bezier curves, e.g. boolean union or intersection, these still have to be done in bezier form. This implies some amount of round-tripping between the two representations, which would introduce numerical drift. However, only the newly created points need to be converted back, because the curvature and tangents elsewhere remain the same.

* * *

This post started from the observation that "symmetric" bezier tangents aren't actually symmetric as you'd expect. Hopefully you found the resulting exploration enlightening.

The practice of showing curvature combs to diagnose problems with splines is really backwards. If we can show a curvature comb, we can also compute an appropriate spline to match the desired curvature.

So beziers as they commonly exist are quite inadequate. We can retrofit a better system to edit them without breaking the expectations of a smooth editing experience, or introducing a new class of curves that behaves very differently.

The code for the diagrams and implementation can be found on GitLab.

Like Bic pens, the design is decades old and they're everywhere. You'll often find them as the default or only choice in various illustration and animation tools. Conceived by Paul de Casteljau in 1959, and refined by Pierre Bézier in the 1960s at Renault, the enduring appeal of the bezier curve lies in its simplicity. items.title: What's next for SpaceX's Starship after epic Flight 15 chopsticks catch?
items.subtitle: Starship may have just made history, but it still has some work to do to get fully up and running.
items.feedText: The megarocket launched on its 15th test flight on Friday (Nov. 13), aiming to pull off a dramatic and unprecedented twofer. items.articleBody:
Starship may have just made history, but it still has some work to do to get fully up and running.

The megarocket [launched on its 15th test flight](https://www.space.com/space-exploration/launches-spacecraft/spacex-starship-flight-15-chopsticks-double-catch-super-heavy-ship) on Friday (Nov. 13), aiming to pull off a dramatic and unprecedented twofer. [SpaceX](https://www.space.com/18853-spacex.html) wanted to bring both [Starship](https://www.space.com/spacex-starship-super-heavy.html) elements — its Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage — back to the launch pad at its Starbase site in Texas to be caught by the tower's "chopstick" arms.

It didn't happen with Super Heavy; the booster [diverted to a Gulf of Mexico splashdown](https://www.space.com/space-exploration/launches-spacecraft/spacex-says-starship-flight-15-booster-aborted-chopsticks-landing-catch-after-launch-due-to-guidance-issue-video) on Friday evening after experiencing a low-fuel alarm. But [Ship came home successfully](https://www.space.com/space-exploration/launches-spacecraft/spacex-chopsticks-catch-starship-upper-stage-flight-14), nestling into the tower's arms in a soft and unprecedented embrace on Saturday afternoon (Nov. 14), 22.5 hours after lifting off.

Long-distance view of Ship's historic landing on Nov. 14, 2026. (Image credit: SpaceX)

SpaceX has [caught Super Heavy](https://www.space.com/space-exploration/private-spaceflight/spacex-loses-starship-upper-stage-again-but-catches-giant-super-heavy-booster-during-flight-8-launch-video) on three test flights to date. But it had never caught a Ship before; indeed, it had never even tried before Saturday. It's tougher and riskier to catch Ship; the upper stage flies much higher and faster than Super Heavy, so its return trip is much more more involved.

Saturday was therefore a very big day for the company.

"That was the holy grail of spaceflight, plummeting through fire to be snatched out of the air by steel," SpaceX spokesperson Dan Huot said during the company's landing webcast on Saturday. "We caught a Starship, and now everything changes."

The [F](https://www.space.com/news/live/spacex-starship-flight-15-live-updates-nov-14-2026-starship-first-double-landing-attempt)[light 15](https://www.space.com/news/live/spacex-starship-flight-15-live-updates-nov-14-2026-starship-first-double-landing-attempt) mission plan gave us a sneak peek at the future: The double catch will be standard on operational Starship missions, as this recovery strategy will enable rapid inspection, refurbishment and reflight of the megarocket, according to SpaceX.

And the company is indeed planning on rapid reflight. [Elon Musk](https://www.space.com/18849-elon-musk.html) has said that SpaceX is targeting 10,000 Starship launches per year by 2030, which works out to more than one liftoff every hour on average.

Why such a mind-boggling cadence? Because SpaceX plans to build megaconstellations far larger than anything circling Earth today. For example, it wants its next-gen Starlink V3 broadband network to consist of [100,000 satellites](https://www.space.com/space-exploration/satellites/spacex-wants-to-launch-100-000-starlink-satellites-to-orbit). And its planned Starmind AI data-center constellation will be 10 times bigger than that, featuring [one million spacecraft](https://www.space.com/space-exploration/satellites/elon-musk-wants-to-put-1-million-ai-satellites-in-space-heres-how-spacex-could-do-it), if all goes to plan.

For perspective: SpaceX's current-gen Starlink network in [low Earth orbit](https://www.space.com/low-earth-orbit) (LEO), by far the largest constellation ever assembled, is about 11,000 strong at the moment.

A look at the 33 Raptor engines of Starship's Super Heavy booster during the vehicle's Flight 15 test launch on Nov. 14, 2026. (Image credit: Josh Dinner, Space.com/Future)

Rocket recovery is only part of the reuse equation, of course; there's also refurbishment and reflight. And that gets us back to the "work left to do" discussion, for SpaceX has yet to demonstrate rapid reflight with either Super Heavy or Ship.

The company has reflown Super Heavy vehicles on two separate occasions. Booster 14 initially launched on Flight 7 in January 2025, then lifted off again on Flight 9 in May of that year. Booster 15 flew on Flight 8 and [Flight 11](https://www.space.com/space-exploration/private-spaceflight/spacex-starship-rocket-flight-11-launch-success), which lifted off in March 2025 and October 2025, respectively.

Several months separated each of these Super Heavy reflights. And SpaceX has yet to reuse a Ship, as it had not caught one during a mission until Saturday.

That could change soon: Before Flight 15 lifted off, Musk said that the company wants to reuse both of its Starship stages. That option may still be on the table for Flight 15's Ship.

And we should expect full reuse to be a priority on Starship test flights over the longer haul, with SpaceX working toward shorter and shorter turnaround times — perhaps until an hourly cadence is in sight, if that goal is indeed achievable.

Over the next few years, most Starship launches will likely be devoted to building out the Starlink V3 and Starmind megaconstellations. But the rocket will also carry people to deep space, if all goes to plan, which will require the checking of another set of boxes.

NASA selected Ship to be the first crewed lunar lander for its [Artemis program](https://www.space.com/artemis-program.html), which aims to establish a base near the lunar south pole by 2032 or so. Current plans call for Ship to land astronauts in that locale for the first time on the [Artemis IV](https://www.space.com/space-exploration/artemis/should-artemis-iv-astronauts-actually-land-near-the-moons-south-pole-artemis-ii-pilot-says-the-lunar-equator-might-be-better) mission, which is targeted to fly in 2028.

SpaceX needs to install a crew cabin and life-support system in Ship to make that happen. The company is working on that now and has made considerable progress, according to NASA. Last month, an [agency presentation](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20260009199/downloads/HLS%20IAC%202026%20Presentation%20FINAL.pdf) reported that SpaceX is on target to finish building "Cabin 1," a full-scale ground prototype of Ship's crew cabin, by the end of the year.

There's another hurdle to clear, however. On all deep-space missions, Ship will need to fill up its fuel tanks after launch, at a "depot" that SpaceX will set up in Earth orbit. (Launching Ship with full tanks is not an option, as it would be incredibly heavy in that case.)

The depot will be filled by "tanker" variants of Ship. [It's unclear](https://www.space.com/space-exploration/artemis/do-we-know-how-many-starship-launches-spacex-will-need-to-get-nasa-astronauts-to-the-moon-no-will-its-refuelling-plan-be-simple-also-no) how many tanker visits will be required for each Ship deep-space mission; outside experts have floated numbers as high as 22, while Musk has cited six to eight as a probable range.

Whatever the actual number, Ship will need to demonstrate proficiency with off-Earth refueling, something it has yet to do. And there's more to it than just a simple rendezvous: Ship's engines run on liquid oxygen and liquid methane, so the propellants must be kept extremely cold throughout the process.

We're likely to see the first refueling test relatively soon, as time is of the essence for SpaceX. If the company can't get Ship ready for the Artemis IV moon landing in 2028, NASA may go with another private lander — Blue Origin's [Blue Moon](https://www.space.com/space-exploration/artemis/when-will-spacex-and-blue-origin-fly-to-the-moon-nasa-reveals-lunar-lander-timelines-and-an-artemis-iii-update), which the agency also contracted for Artemis missions.

All of this is to say that, while Flight 15 was a big success for Starship and SpaceX, there's a lot of work left to do — and a lot for space fans to watch for over the coming weeks and months.

items.articleBody:
Seit drei Wochen klappt CNET das faltbare iPhone Duo im Livestream mit einer Faltmaschine auf und zu, bislang mehr als 451.000 Mal. Obwohl das Gerät weiterhin funktioniert, hat das Scharnier inzwischen so viel Spiel, dass sich das Display in der Testmaschine nicht mehr ganz öffnet.

Fotocredit: Apple

## Drei Wochen Dauertest im Livestream

CNET lässt das iPhone Duo von einer Maschine namens „Fold-a-Phone“ auf- und zuklappen und überträgt den Test live im Netz. Laut den Testern wirkte das Scharnier nach etwa 390.000 Faltvorgängen erstmals lockerer. Bei rund 440.300 Faltvorgängen hatte sich die Mechanik dann so weit verändert, dass das Display nicht mehr ganz aufklappte, bevor die Testmaschine es wieder schloss. Seitdem rastet es auch nicht mehr spürbar ein. Von Hand lässt sich das Display weiterhin vollständig aufklappen, während in der Maschine fünf bis zehn Grad bis zur ganz geöffneten Stellung fehlen.

Den Test setzt CNET trotzdem fort, zumal das iPhone Duo nach wie vor funktioniert und sein Display in anderen Winkeln stehen bleibt. Er endet erst, wenn sich das Gerät nicht mehr einschalten lässt, das Display schwarz bleibt oder die Sensoren die Stellung des Displays nicht mehr richtig erkennen. Bis dahin läuft der Livestream werktags von 19 bis 23 Uhr deutscher Zeit.

Apple hat weder Ergebnisse eigener Scharniertests veröffentlicht noch angegeben, wie viele Faltvorgänge das iPhone Duo aushalten soll. Einen Anhaltspunkt bietet das Galaxy Z Fold7, dessen Display wie die OLED-Panels des iPhone Duo von Samsung Display stammt und in einem zertifizierten Test eines unabhängigen Labors 500.000 Faltvorgänge überstanden hat. Obwohl Apple vermutlich kein Standardpanel von dem Hersteller verwendet, spricht der bisherige Testverlauf dafür, dass das Display des iPhone Duo einen ähnlichen Wert erreicht.

Wie lange das Gerät im Alltag hält, hängt allerdings vom Display und vom Scharnier zusammen ab. Schon die bisher erreichten 450.000 Faltvorgänge entsprechen einer Nutzungsdauer von mehr als zehn Jahren, wenn man das iPhone Duo 100-mal am Tag auf- und zuklappt.

items.articleBody:
**Nach dem Willen einer britischen Initiative sollen iPhones und andere Mobilgeräte künftig sämtliche Fotos und Videos prüfen. auch bei Erwachsenen. Beim Kinderschutz auf dem Smartphone erhöht Großbritannien weiter den Druck. Erst im September hat die Regierung angekündigt, Apple und Google per Gesetz zu Schutzfiltern für Minderjährige zu verpflichten.**

## Politik erhöht den Druck

Einer parteiübergreifenden Gruppe aus Unterhaus und Oberhaus reicht das nicht. Wie der britische [Observer](https://observer.co.uk/news/national/article/fight-to-block-child-sexual-abuse-images-unites-peers-and-mps-in-cross-party-campaign) berichtet, fordert sie verpflichtende Bildfilter auf allen Smartphones und Tablets, die Darstellungen sexualisierter Gewalt gegen Kinder erkennen und blockieren. Gelten soll das für jeden Nutzer, unabhängig vom Alter.

An der Spitze des Vorstoßes stehen der konservative Lord John Nash und die Labour-Abgeordnete Jess Phillips. Phillips war bis Mai Safeguarding-Ministerin und warf der Regierung bei ihrem Rücktritt unter anderem vor, beim Schutz auf Geräteebene zu zögern. Geht es nach der Gruppe, prüfen iOS, iPadOS und Android Bilder und Videos automatisch und machen verdächtige Inhalte unkenntlich, bevor sie auf dem Display erscheinen. KI-generiertes Material ist ausdrücklich eingeschlossen, außerdem soll das System das Erstellen solcher Inhalte und entsprechende Livestreams verhindern. Bereits verkaufte Geräte sollen per Pflichtupdate nachgerüstet werden. Übernimmt die Regierung den Vorschlag nicht, will Nash ihn als Änderungsantrag zum geplanten Gesetz zur nationalen Sicherheit einbringen. Mit ähnlichen Anträgen ist er im Oberhaus bereits gescheitert. Als Begründung führen die Initiatoren Zahlen der [Internet Watch Foundation](https://www.iwf.org.uk/annual-data-insights-report-2025/executive-summary/) an. Die Organisation hat 2025 mehr als 312.000 Meldungen mit Missbrauchsmaterial bestätigt, ein Plus von sieben Prozent. Bei KI-generierten Missbrauchsvideos stieg die Zahl von 13 auf rund 3.440.

## Überraschend viele Fragen bleiben offen

Offen lassen die Vorschläge, wie zuverlässig die Erkennung arbeiten müsste und wie mit Fehlalarmen umzugehen ist. Wie häufig solche Systeme danebenliegen, zeigt eine Zahl des Bundeskriminalamts: 2024 war fast jeder zweite der rund 206.000 aus den USA weitergeleiteten Hinweise strafrechtlich nicht relevant. Apple kennt die Debatte gut. 2021 plante der iPhone-Konzern einen Abgleich von iCloud-Fotos mit bekanntem Missbrauchsmaterial und gab das Vorhaben nach heftiger Kritik Ende 2022 auf. Seither setzt Cupertino auf den Kommunikationsschutz, der Nacktbilder in Kinderaccounts direkt auf dem Gerät erkennt und unscharf darstellt. Mit iOS 27 ist er für alle Accounts unter 18 Jahren automatisch aktiv. Datenschützer lehnen verpflichtendes Scannen auf dem Gerät seit Jahren ab. Ihr Argument: Es untergräbt die Ende-zu-Ende-Verschlüsselung und ließe sich technisch auf andere Inhalte ausweiten. Ob aus der Initiative ein Gesetz wird, ist derzeit offen. Für Apple wäre es nicht der erste Konflikt mit London: Anfang 2025 hat der Hersteller den erweiterten Datenschutz für iCloud für britische Neukunden zurückgezogen, statt eine Hintertür einzubauen.

items.articleBody:
> In a “weak links” model of production, where tasks are complements, the gains from automation tend to arrive slowly because output is constrained by the least productive tasks. But the same complementarity makes attacks more harmful and easier to execute. For example, with an elasticity of substitution across tasks of 0.2, automating tasks worth 1 percent of GDP with a tenfold increase in productivity raises output by less than one percent, while cutting their productivity tenfold lowers output by 68 percent on impact. Whena larger AI sector simultaneously makes AI models more capable and attacks more likely, the positive productivity spillover is negligible compared with the potential damage, so the market overinvests in AI. In a weak-link economy, the costs and benefits from AI can be extremely asymmetric.

That is from [a recent “in progress” manuscript](https://christophertonetti.com/files/papers/JonesTonetti_WeakLinksRisk.pdf) by Charles I. Jones and Christopher Tonetti. Via [Lukas Freund](https://x.com/_LukasFreund_/status/2121672282963583087).

items.articleBody:
*Housekeeping:*

- There will be a reader meetup in SF on December 10: [RSVP here.](https://luma.com/mk1c03jk)
- I’ll be in Stockholm on November 26 and made [a Luma event if someone wants to meet up](https://luma.com/8ga6l729). You can also dm me on Substack.

If you read writing advice, you’ll often stumble upon all of these rather abstract rules, such as “show, don’t tell,” “open the essay with a concrete story to engage people,” and so on. I don’t find advice like that useful at all. These sorts of maxims remind me of the small notes I might jot down to myself to remember the directions to a friend’s house—“left, right, past the oak tree, right.” Well, that might describe the right way, but it is a very rough map of the terrain, and if it turns out that the person who wrote the notes forgot to mention something—or perhaps was going somewhere other than you—their advice will lead you completely astray.

To develop a good toolbox, I find it much more fruitful to take the texts that I feel do whatever I want to learn best and read them slowly, repeatedly, with a pencil in hand. It’s like taking a slow, attentive walk around the neighborhood, getting a deep *feeling* for the landscape, for what it means to write at the highest levels. I will usually form a few theories about why the text is so powerful and I might spot a few techniques I can put into my toolbox, but these theories and techniques will be much more idiosyncratic and tentative than the ones I get from consuming writing advice: I will create tools that are meaningful to *my* projects, and my taste, and I will hold the tools with a light hand, knowing full well that they are just a rough guess, derived from a limited reading.

Last weekend, I did such a close reading of the piece that David Foster Wallace wrote about John McCain’s failed campaign for the Republican presidential nomination in 2000—the one that was originally published as “The Weasel, Twelve Monkeys and the Shrub,” a sprawling ~15,700-word essay in the April 13 issue of *Rolling Stone,* and later republished in a three-times-as-long “director’s cut” ebook called, first, *Up, Simba*, and later, *McCain’s Promise*. It is a New Journalism-derived sort of essay-reportage hybrid, where DFW travels around with the McCain campaign’s press bus, fails to interview any of the main players, and instead hangs around with the cameramen and sound technicians, but does little of the standard journalistic scene-setting and interview-quoting, in favor of a kind of writing that is a crossover between diary and essay.

I have read the book-length version of *McCain’s Promise* four times, I think, and the short version, once or twice. The immediate excuse for the last two + one rereads was that I wanted to understand how DFW integrates interviews and scene-setting into his essayistic reflections (and for the answer to that see this footnote1), but what I ended up focusing most on during the actual reading was the question: how on earth does he manage to make the reading so engaging and have such strong narrative momentum when most of it is just very long and detailed descriptions of the interior of a bus and the different kinds of phones people use on the bus and so on?

#### How DFW creates narrative momentum
