items.articleBody:
Illustration by Shoshana Gordon/ProPublica

On the night of Feb. 15, 2022, Robert Maddox Jr., a rookie cop in a small Alabama town, called his colleague in a panic. His wife was about three months pregnant and bleeding heavily. They needed someone to watch their two sleeping children while they went to the hospital.

Headland police Officer James “Bo” Knight arrived with his wife. He had been serving as a mentor of sorts to Robert, who had just recently joined the department, and had urged him to reach out if he ever needed help.

The situation Knight encountered was a heavy one. Robert had something in a plastic bag that looked to Knight like fetal remains. His wife stood by silently. Robert said he’d be back as soon as possible, that he was taking both his wife and the bag to the hospital.

When the couple returned three hours later, Robert was holding a white container.

“They put my fucking baby in a box,” he said.

Investigators soon began building a case that it was Robert who caused the miscarriage. About six weeks after she lost the pregnancy, Brittany Maddox reported her husband for assaulting her before and after she went to the hospital. She first went to an abuse-prevention organization, which connected her to the police and helped her get a protective order from the court. She provided the Houston County judge with a description of how Robert choked and beat her in front of their 1- and 2-year-old children just before the miscarriage, as well as pictures taken starting the following week of marks on her neck. She handed over text messages from Robert in which he promised not to hurt her again and begged her to consider how his imprisonment would hurt their family.

“Being honest is going to get us both screwed,” he wrote. “The truth is going to give me locked up.”

Then, the Headland Police Department colleague who had offered to help Robert stepped forward. Knight gave a sworn statement to investigators in Dothan, the nearby city where the young couple rented an apartment. He recounted how, weeks after the incident, Robert confided in him that he had hit Brittany in the stomach, choked her and pushed her to the ground.

“I asked him how many times he has done this,” Knight said in his statement. “He stated many.”

According to the statement, Knight asked when he had last hurt her — and Robert responded “the night before you kept my kids.”

In Alabama, the legal implications of causing a miscarriage are severe. Politicians and prosecutors have long proclaimed their mission to defend the unborn. The state has gone further than almost every other to embrace “fetal personhood” — the legal concept that embryos and fetuses deserve the same rights and protections as children. The result is that people charged in Alabama with harming a fetus face especially lengthy prison sentences.

The authorities came down hard on Robert, at least at first. He was charged with murder.

But in the years that followed, Houston County’s criminal justice system would prove lenient for him. Robert was released on bond about five weeks after his arrest and never again saw the inside of a jail or prison cell.

His case stands in stark contrast to dozens of other fetal personhood prosecutions in Houston County, which sits in the corner of the state near the borders of Florida and Georgia. Those defendants were pregnant women. They were charged not for actually harming their unborn babies but for potentially endangering them — not by violence but by using drugs.

In all but one of those cases, which date back nearly two decades, their babies survived. Some of the women spent months in jail and even went to prison.

A former nurse, who had been battling a meth addiction for years, was arrested in 2018 after she tested positive for drug use while in labor and wound up spending nearly 10 months in prison. Another woman, who also tested positive at the hospital where she gave birth, ended up in jail for four months in 2024 — and said many fellow inmates were women who’d been arrested for using drugs while pregnant.

Courtney Haney at a family member’s home last month in Dothan, Alabama. Her daughter was born healthy, but Haney spent four months in jail for prenatal drug use. A. Wallace for ProPublica

Houston County District Attorney Russ Goodman, who took office in January 2023, said in an email that his office has made efforts to help the women by recommending addiction treatment as part of their sentences. He also said some were rearrested and imprisoned for violating probation — or never completed the treatment offered by the court.

“During my term it is rare that we would sentence a defendant in these types of cases to a straight prison sentence,” Goodman said, “unless of course there were other extenuating circumstances, such as prior criminal history.”

As for Robert Maddox, Goodman said that the evidence against him was inconclusive, and he questioned the prior district attorney’s decision to seek an indictment. “It pained me as a prosecutor that I was not to be able to seek justice in this case,” he said.

Robert declined an interview but said in an email, “I was made out to be someone I wasn’t.” He did not respond when pressed to elaborate. ProPublica later sent him a detailed list of the allegations against him. He replied, “That is not what happened.” In response to a follow-up email, he said his wife had no bruising or marks at the hospital.

“If I was abusive and abused her then took her to the hospital they would have saw the marks and not let me leave with her,” he wrote in an email.

Lourdes Rivera, president of the advocacy group Pregnancy Justice, said her organization has identified [2,298 cases](https://www.pregnancyjusticeus.org/rise-of-pregnancy-criminalization-report/) of women arrested since 2006 on charges related to their pregnancy. Most of those were for drug use and are concentrated in Oklahoma, South Carolina and Alabama. Rivera said the numbers of women prosecuted for pregnancy loss appear to be [on the rise](https://www.pregnancyjusticeus.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Fall-2026-Data-Update.pdf)compared with the years before the U.S. Supreme Court overturned the right to an abortion.

“Law enforcement is using laws that were never intended to apply to pregnancy to investigate, arrest and punish women,” Rivera said. “And it’s only getting worse.”

Robert’s promise not to hurt Brittany again after the miscarriage lasted about a week, she said. She would later tell a judge that he began hitting and choking her again, and photos from that time show bruising on her neck and eye. In that time, something shifted.

“I started hating him when I saw my baby dead,” she wrote in response to ProPublica’s questions.

She said it took her several weeks to come forward because she had to work through complicated feelings about the loss of both her pregnancy and a husband she still loved despite the hatred that was building. She also wasn’t sure if she and her daughters could safely leave him.

About a week before she went to the authorities, she got a text from her husband asking if she’d give him one more chance. “I can’t give you your baby back,” he wrote. “That’s something I’m always going to live with knowing I did that.”

For help in [English](https://www.thehotline.org/) or [Spanish](https://espanol.thehotline.org/), call the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 800-799-7233 or text “start” to 88788.

Asked about the text, Robert wrote to ProPublica, “I was referring to having to pull my kid out a toilet I couldn’t believe I had to do that. It was painful emotionally.”

Robert had started working as an officer at the Headland Police Department about four months earlier. Brittany worried the other officers would side with her husband, but she quashed her fears and reached out on social media to several of them anyway. She said Robert went into her account and deleted the messages she’d sent. But it was too late.

Knight, one of the officers she messaged, confronted Robert, who admitted that he had hit Brittany in the stomach before the miscarriage, the officer later told the Dothan police. Robert furiously messaged Brittany.

“If you want me to go to jail keep accusing me of it,” he wrote. “Just know I love you and it will never happen again but I think I’m getting fired.”

Domestic abuse is a leading killer of pregnant women. And for every fatal case, there are an estimated 70 nonfatal ones. Researchers have found that [almost 13%](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38265064/) of women surveyed experienced domestic violence during pregnancy.

Nonfatal cases usually go unreported, according to Maeve Wallace, an expert on domestic violence at the University of Arizona. The same goes for miscarriages, which often happen at home and may leave no medical record. That can make it difficult to determine how often abuse causes miscarriage, she said.

### Read More

[These Women Were Trying to Escape Domestic Abuse. ICE Detained Them Instead.](https://www.propublica.org/article/domestic-violence-immigrant-victims-ice-detention)

Brittany said her relationship with Robert had been turbulent from the start. She was still in high school when they started dating, and she uprooted her life to relocate to his hometown of Dothan. She said he started physically hurting her months into the relationship and that it escalated after the move. Brittany found herself isolated in Alabama, where life revolved almost entirely around her husband, two young children and the couple’s car-detailing business.

“Robert would also hurt me if things weren’t done perfectly or if any issues happened,” Brittany wrote.

Unlike many other victims of domestic violence, she hounded the police and prosecutors to take her case seriously after the miscarriage.

Cases against abusers accused of causing pregnancy loss can be tricky to prove, often requiring evidence that the abuser intentionally struck the victim in the stomach and testimony from a forensic pathologist linking the violence to the pregnancy loss. In one strange turn, a grand jury in a city outside of Birmingham indicted a woman for starting a fight that led to her being shot in the stomach and suffering a miscarriage.

It’s easier and more common to pursue charges against defendants when they are accused of killing both a pregnant woman and her fetus.

Laws don’t provide an easy path for punishing abusers of pregnant women, especially when the baby survives, according to law professor Mary Ziegler, who teaches at the University of California, Davis. But laws do make prosecution of pregnant women who use drugs astonishingly easy. Those cases come to light almost automatically — and there is little opportunity to challenge them. Hospitals frequently administer drug tests to pregnant women and notify child protective services of positive results. Those agencies often turn over that information to police in Alabama, where drug use is not grounds just for a child welfare investigation but for a felony charge.

The women are prosecuted under Alabama’s chemical endangerment law, which makes it illegal to expose children to drugs. Although the 2006 law initially was designed to address the dangers of home-based meth labs, prosecutors almost immediately began using it against pregnant women.

ProPublica identified more than 40 pregnant women arrested in Houston County since 2009 on chemical endangerment charges after testing positive for drugs. An analysis of court data also found that the county prosecuted women for chemical endangerment at one of the highest rates in the state, though the data doesn’t specify whether the cases involved pregnancies.

In one case, a 24-year-old whose newborn tested positive for methadone and marijuana received a five-year prison sentence in 2009. Another woman, who’d been convicted for exposing her fetus to THC in 2013, had her probation revoked for possessing synthetic marijuana and spent about nine months in prison.

Pat Jones, who was Houston County’s district attorney at the time of these cases, did not respond to a request for comment.

According to Ziegler, there is a pronounced unevenness in who gets punished under statutes that protect fetuses.

“The versions of personhood that are enshrined in our laws have tended to focus on the conduct of women,” she said.

Courtney Haney grew up in Dothan but left at age 18 to join a high-pressure sales crew that traveled across the country, selling boxes of frozen meat door-to-door. The work was stressful, and it attracted misfits and risk-takers. Several of her colleagues used drugs, but Haney became pregnant unexpectedly and stayed clean.

Her daughter was born healthy, arriving exactly on her due date. But soon, cracks appeared in her relationship with the father, and he split, taking the baby with him. When her colleagues moved on to other cities, Haney remained in Denver to look for her child. She had no family there and no friends. Her despair became overwhelming. She turned to drugs and became homeless, eventually losing custody.

Almost a year later, Haney found out she was pregnant again and returned to Dothan in 2020 with a full-blown addiction to heroin. She went to the hospital with contractions the week before she gave birth and knew she would test positive for drugs. She also said no one offered her options for drug treatment, even after she asked for help. Instead, hospital staff stabilized and discharged her. She kept using until she returned to give birth, when she was drug-tested again.

“I was holding my daughter in my hands and the police walked in,” Haney said.

They asked her questions, and she hoped they might show mercy and allow her to go home with her child. After they told her she might be charged with a felony for exposing her fetus to drugs, she burst into tears.

“I answered honestly, thinking that if I’ve answered honestly they wouldn’t press charges,” she said. “And that was pointless.”

To avoid more criminal charges, Haney drove out of state to give birth to her two younger children. A. Wallace for ProPublica

She was arrested for chemical endangerment three months later.

For women struggling with addiction during pregnancy, a chemical endangerment arrest can initiate a cycle of devastating court fees, imprisonment on probation violations and even additional charges. And the separation from their newborns and other children can drive them deeper into addiction. Unlike in many other counties, Houston County does not offer a drug court program, which allows defendants to get substance-abuse treatment instead of prison time and avoid a felony on their record.

A woman who was about seven months’ pregnant was arrested in Houston County the very same day as Robert Maddox, in 2022. She was briefly jailed for violating probation stemming from a past chemical endangerment conviction. She then faced additional felony charges when, weeks later, she tested positive for cocaine at the hospital where she gave birth. She later received a five-year sentence and wound up at Tutwiler Prison for Women.

Her release date is right before Christmas in 2028.

Haney had no felony convictions, but a sentencing report recommended against straight probation due to charges in other states that had been dismissed. Ultimately, the Houston County district attorney’s office offered a plea deal for a lesser charge and just over a year of probation.

Haney struggled to abide by the conditions of her sentence. She did not complete court-ordered drug treatment and failed to report to her probation officer several times. As a result, she was jailed for a total of four months.

Many of the other women jailed with her also had been arrested on charges of chemical endangerment as a result of failing drug tests during childbirth.

“Whenever I went to jail, that’s where I met most of them,” Haney said. “There’s a whole lot of them in Houston County.”

Haney became pregnant two more times while she was addicted. For her third child, she traveled to nearby Georgia to give birth, and then to Florida for her fourth. Neither state arrests women for prenatal drug use at the same high rate as Alabama.

Xaviera Smith, a former nurse and mother of three from Tennessee, said she knew she would be arrested before she even gave birth in Houston County to her youngest son in 2018. Smith couldn’t deny the results of the drug test that had been administered while she was in labor. She had been battling a meth addiction for years.

She said that, fortunately, her baby was born healthy and did not need to go to the neonatal intensive care unit for drug withdrawal.

Smith had a court-appointed attorney who negotiated a deal on her chemical endangerment charge. She was sentenced to 10 years but could avoid prison by serving time through the local work-release program.

“I just went to court and took what they gave me,” Smith said. ”There’s nothing I really could do.”

After violating the terms of work release, she ended up in prison for nearly a year.

Brittany Maddox believed the case against her husband was a straightforward one. She felt there was solid evidence that the abuse caused her miscarriage. But the effort proved to be harder than she anticipated.

A few months after his arrest, the grand jury declined to indict him for murder, opting instead for a lesser charge of manslaughter.

The indictment alleged that Robert had “recklessly” caused the death of his wife’s fetus by “punching her in the stomach with a closed fist.” The maximum punishment would be 20 years in prison.

As Robert waited for his day in court, he asked the judge to relax some of the conditions of his bond. He had lost his job with the Headland police because of his wife’s claims of abuse and had started washing cars again. He wanted the court to remove the ankle monitor so he could more easily travel to work in Florida, which is near Dothan.

From her home out of state, Brittany had been calling the district attorney’s office once or twice a month to ensure authorities kept an eye on her estranged husband’s whereabouts. She was shocked to learn of his out-of-state travel request — not from prosecutors but from a news story. For the first time since his arrest, she felt unsafe.

A judge denied his motion to remove the ankle monitor but granted his request to commute to north Florida.

Brittany stayed in touch with prosecutors and began to mentally prepare for trial. She said that as months stretched into years, the conversations with them began to shift. They asked her how she felt about a plea deal, and she said she would be open to it, as long as the charge related to her miscarriage wasn’t dropped completely.

“I told them I could push through a trial emotionally,” Brittany wrote.

Finally, almost four years after Robert was arrested, his attorney brokered a plea deal with prosecutors. He would plead guilty to domestic violence, and the prosecution would recommend the manslaughter charge be dismissed.

Goodman, the district attorney, told ProPublica that he would not have been able to prove at trial that Robert committed manslaughter. “There was never any evidence that tied the actions of the defendant to the death of the baby,” he said, adding that “no expert could tie a causal connection.”

He also said he explained to Brittany that “we would not have moved forward on the manslaughter case” had he been in office when his predecessor chose to seek an indictment against Robert.

Brittany said if Goodman believed the charge should be dropped, he should have done it sooner, instead of having her spend years preparing for trial.

“The charge being dropped four years after he was arrested as part of a plea deal makes no sense to me,” she said. “That wrecked me in a lot of ways, more than the times I laid in bed for days after he hurt me.”

On May 18, 2026, Robert appeared before a judge in a Houston County courtroom. Brittany attended the hearing as well. She had traveled to Alabama for all of the hearings, even though she still feared being in the same room with Robert.

After all that waiting, the sentencing felt surprisingly short to her. When the judge moved to dismiss the most serious charge, he didn’t say the word manslaughter or mention the miscarriage. Brittany said she tried to ask questions about the deal, but she wasn’t sworn in, and the judge quickly moved on.

“The victim and the defendant were in a verbal dispute whereas the defendant was alleged to throw the victim down and choke her,” the judge said. “The state alleges that this occurred in front of their minor children as well.”

The judge went on to say that the presence of the children might have increased Robert’s punishment to a minimum six months’ imprisonment. But because he was a first-time offender, that minimum didn’t apply.

The judge sentenced him to five years’ probation and fined him about $3,000, which he could pay off at $50 a month. Then the judge added one more thing: anger management classes, to be completed through the court referral office.

items.articleBody:
rune bosse’s lung trees imagine a forest on life support

Danish artist Rune Bosse places living trees on artificial life support in Lung Trees, an installation presented at the Danish Architecture Center in Copenhagen as part of its Age of Nature exhibition, which ran through September 2026. Each tree stands inside a transparent, inflated plastic enclosure, and is surrounded by mechanical equipment and artificial lighting. With their branches reaching toward overhead lamps, each tree seems to have been removed from the forest and placed under intensive care.

The installation imagines a future in which trees might depend on technology to survive, even as humans continue to depend on the ecological systems that trees help sustain. It reverses a relationship we tend to take for granted. Forests have long been described as the lungs of the planet, absorbing carbon dioxide through photosynthesis and releasing oxygen. Here, Bosse gives those lungs a mechanical counterpart, and suggests a world in which the natural systems supporting human life might themselves require artificial support.

Lungetræ / Lungenbaum, Neue Nationalgalerie, Berlin, 2025. image © Victoria Tomaschko

transparent chambers breathe around living trees

The installation brings together living vegetation and an exposed network of machines. Transparent plastic sheeting stretches over metal frames, enclosing the trees while allowing visitors to see the soil and branches inside. Artificial lights illuminate the foliage, while equipment supplies air to the enclosed environment. The temporary structures have the practical appearance of makeshift greenhouses, although their association with medical equipment gives them a more unsettling character.

In a related 2025 presentation at Berlin’s Neue Nationalgalerie, titled Lungetræ / Lungenbaum, Bosse made the breathing movement particularly visible. A living tree and a section of forest floor were enclosed within a flexible PVC membrane attached to a metal framework. At regular intervals, a respirator pushed air into the structure, causing the plastic to expand and slowly collapse around the tree. The movement resembles the inflation of a giant lung, giving physical form to the invisible exchange of gases between a tree and its surroundings.

Lungetræ / Lungenbaum, Neue Nationalgalerie, Berlin, 2025. image © Victoria Tomaschko

making art with living forests

Bosse’s interest in trees extends well beyond the gallery. Alongside his training at the Royal Danish Academy of Fine Arts, the artist studied forestry and nature management, developing a practice that follows the growth of living plants over time. At Oremandsgaard, an estate in southern Denmark, he has established an outdoor forest laboratory where he experiments with shaping trees as they grow. Some are bent into unusual forms, while others are guided to grow together. Their final shapes emerge over years, influenced by the conditions of the surrounding landscape.

This work grew partly from his frustration with bringing natural materials into museums, where plants often have to be cut, dried or preserved before they can be exhibited. His outdoor experiments allow trees to remain alive and continue changing long after the artist’s initial intervention. Lung Trees approaches the same relationship from a different direction. Inside the gallery, keeping the trees alive becomes part of the artwork itself, exposing the equipment and artificial conditions that make their temporary existence possible.

Træfald, HEART Museum, Herning, Denmark, 2022 | image © David Stjernholm, Rune Bosse

who keeps whom alive?

The installation touches on an uncomfortable contradiction in the way humans approach ecological preservation. By enclosing the trees and supplying them with artificial conditions, Bosse creates an image of protection that also suggests dependency. The machinery appears to care for the living organisms, yet the entire arrangement places their survival within a system designed and operated by humans. The trees remain living participants in the work, although their relationship with the surrounding environment has been fundamentally altered.

Bosse first developed Lungetræer in 2019, and its more recent presentations give the work a continuing relevance amid growing concerns about biodiversity loss and the deterioration of ecosystems. The installation offers a speculative glimpse of what technological preservation might look like when ecological conditions can no longer support life on their own. Its most unsettling quality comes from the simplicity of the scene.

A living tree stands inside a plastic chamber while a machine pushes air around it. The visitor watches the artificial lung expand and contract, confronted with the possibility that the relationship between humans and forests could one day become this fragile.

Træfald, HEART Museum, Herning, Denmark, 2022 | image © David Stjernholm, Rune Bosse

Træfald, HEART Museum, Herning, Denmark, 2022 | image © David Stjernholm, Rune Bosse

items.articleBody:
Note on method: This essay was written through an AI-enhanced process, as were my previous columns here. The argument, the structure, the successive revisions and the final judgement are mine. I developed the line of thought in Polish and used two AI systems, ChatGPT 6.1 and Claude (Anthropic’s Fable 5.1), as critical assistance: to test formulations, to flag overstatement and redundancy, to check transitions, and to help transcreate the Polish text into English. One Claude instance worked throughout in the anti-dogmatic register I have borrowed from Kołakowski since my first column: accept the thesis generously, then examine it sceptically, then say what survives. Because the essay rests on events of the past ten days, the models also ran successive fact-checks against current sources; their own knowledge of 2026 was out of date and had to be corrected several times, which is a useful reminder of what such assistance can and cannot do. My instructions asked the models to challenge the argument rather than flatter it, to hit both sides of the political divide wherever the criticism applied, and to keep the English natural while preserving my voice.

In October 1978 Leszek Kołakowski published a short credo in Encounter under the title “How to Be a Conservative-Liberal-Socialist”. He took its motto from a Warsaw tram, where a conductor used to shout what he rendered as “Please step forward to the rear!”, and he proposed it as the slogan of a mighty International that will never exist, because it cannot promise people that they will be happy. I referred to that essay a month ago, writing here about relations between Canada, Europe and the United States. I return to it today because history has added another chapter.

The Democrats won, and won as they have not in a generation: as of 8 November they hold at least 54 seats in the Senate, with counting still under way in Mississippi and Alaska, and 254 seats to 162 in the House, with 19 districts uncalled. The background is the war with Iran, fought since 28 February, and the price of petrol, which rose from $2.98 a gallon before the war to more than $4 in the spring and still cost that much on election day. Even Vice President Vance had the honesty to write that the problem was not turnout but the fact that people who voted for Trump in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026, and among the causes he named the war with Iran. We know whose decision that was.

One of the three traditions named in the credo, the conservative one, lost, and the first reflex of its present custodians was to do what they had been doing for the past ten years. Four days after the midterms the President called on the Department of Justice to deal with the Democrats who, having won, had announced impeachments of members of his cabinet; he called those announcements extortion, offering no evidence that anyone had been threatened. This essay, however, is not about why the right lost. It is about what is left of it, and about what in it was left-wing.

I use Kołakowski’s measure, though I am not sure I have the nerve to enroll in his International, since the founder himself ruled that it will never come into being. But institutions that do not exist have an advantage over those that do: they need not win elections, they issue no muddled statements after defeats, and they let us picture problems whole and ask questions that no existing institution will ask, because each has something to lose. Kołakowski called the components of his credo a set of regulative ideas, Kant’s term: not a description of what is, but a measure held up against what is. Let me declare that I write this essay as a man who cannot stand his own country’s right; the reader gets my prejudice at the outset. But a negative attitude to the custodians need not determine one’s attitude to the deposit, that is, in the old sense of something held in trust, to the handful of principles the right was supposed to keep, which I shall speak up for in the second half of this text. So the question is what, of everything the right calls important, we must not throw away, even if those who were supposed to guard it first betrayed it and then lost anyway.

Two Rights

“The right” means several things, and most arguments about it consist in the speaker sliding between the meanings. There is the right as a disposition: to prefer the known to the unknown. There is the right as a doctrine: claims about human nature, about the limits of reason, about evil not being something you can remove from the world like a defect in a machine. And there is the right as a coalition, in which, since 1955, libertarians, traditionalists and anti-communists have shared one tent. Over the years that coalition grew into a mosaic of conservatisms, from the salon to the folk variety, which formed a unity of sorts; a unity built on tensions, hard compromises and contradictions first passed over in silence and then swelling, on mutual dishonesty and a growing tolerance for dishonesty. On top of that, traditional conservatism lost its cultural appeal for its own voters. This right, made up of disposition, doctrine and coalition together, I shall call the old mainstream right. For many years it held, in the United States, a monopoly on the deposit this text is about.

There is also a second right, and it was under its leadership that the Republicans lost on 3 November. It is called populist, but the word papers over the phenomenon and explains nothing; everyone who wants to win appeals to the people. Every ideology has at its source some first question, first fear, first reflex. I would make a fairly safe bet that ideologies become most dangerous, and the worst versions of themselves, when they degenerate to their simplest form, when they give up their own tradition and their own experience. So whenever we hear too often about a return to “true roots”, we should start paying attention.

That, in my view, is the heart of the trouble with the big MAGA tent. It reacts with its first reflex. It answers fears, and in doing so throws away its own traditions and principles, degrading its own ideology and its own political camp down to the roots. In certain respects it becomes so conservative that it discards a large part of conservatism’s own achievement.

A reflex becomes a view only when it turns into a claim that can be tested and refuted; fear of immigration is a reflex, while the statement that immigration lowered wages in construction by such and such a figure is already work, because it is a bet you can lose.

The old mainstream right, not free of those reflexes itself, nonetheless had institutions and milieux that turned fear into knowledge of what must not be touched; the right of the first reflex turned fear into a goal that has to be kept alive.

Curiously, an apparent paradox followed. The nationalist right founded an international of global reach. CPAC has met in Budapest since 2022, most recently in March, a month before Orbán lost an election after sixteen years in power. Bolsonaro, sentenced to twenty-seven years for an attempted coup, and Trump understood each other without an interpreter whenever the talk turned to pardons for their own people, contracts for the family and courts to be remade. The name “right of the first reflex” belongs above all to those who service the reflex, because the reflex itself is no more to blame than fuel is.

It should of course be said at this point that the left has its own temptations and passions, an anger at injustice that goes feral just as easily; and the liberal centre has its contempt for those who know less and do not fit the meritocratic checkboxes. My “cannot stand” from the opening probably also stems from the limits of the liberal way of thinking.

A Code without an Ethics

On 25 July 2016, in Philadelphia, Michelle Obama said: “When they go low, we go high.” Coming from her, it was a decent thing to say; nobody has the right to demand that the person cheated roll in the mud with the cheat. The trouble began when a personal sentence became a party’s code, because a code, as Kołakowski showed in “Ethics without a Code”, keeps the conscience safe and supplies moral comfort without changing the conditions that produce the conflict. “We go high”, adopted by a party, says little about the opponent but begins to build the group around a new criterion of hierarchy: position is set by moral superiority over those outside, and to stand high you need someone to keep down. The grim joke is that Europe had tested where that logic ends only a few weeks earlier, in June 2016, before the sentence was spoken. I am not claiming that one followed from the other; I am claiming that it is the same mechanism, shown twice in one summer. Voters who had been told for years that their fears were shameful voted for Brexit, and on the Continent voters began to vote for anyone who did not tell them to be ashamed. This is not an argument for relieving voters of moral responsibility for the decisions they make; that certain groups’ fears are justified does not by itself mean their political demands should be met. But persistent blindness to those fears ends with somebody else harvesting them. In 2026 the Democrats won on petrol, among other things, but also on a message about the cost of living, which Hakeem Jeffries had put at the centre of the campaign as early as July, and not on going high; and, unlike in 2024, voters trusted them more than the Republicans on the economy. If you are fighting someone brutal who reasons in the logic of violence, going high is not enough; you have to go highly focused.

The year 2016 also produced a second code without an ethics, though merely placing the two side by side is already too much symmetry. “The Flight 93 Election” appeared on 5 September in the Claremont Review of Books, written by Michael Anton under the pseudonym Publius Decius Mus. Flight 93 was the hijacked plane of 11 September 2001 on which the passengers attacked the cockpit and all of them died, but the hijackers never reached their target; Anton wrote that the choice in 2016 was the same: charge the cockpit or die. Where Michelle Obama’s sentence tempted some with a sense of their own elite standing, this one released every moral brake. On one side, then, we got people with an irritating posture whose long-term effects will doubtless be harmful. On the other, an assault that does not intend to ask what happens after landing, because in an apocalypse there is no choice, there is necessity, there is decision, a word that in this context should send a shiver down the spine, until out of it is born a duty to act. To act outside all rules and procedures, because every action in this mode of thinking borders on the state of exception. That is why these people do not feel compromised: they were not choosing, they were saving the plane. And an apocalypse does not wear out. In Anton’s metaphor the assault succeeded: Trump won in November 2016 and took office in January 2017, so the state of exception should have ended. It did not: in 2020 the election was “stolen”, 2024 was “the final battle”, and four days after 3 November 2026 the new threat to the republic turned out to be announced impeachments, which had to be reported to the prosecutors.

A Coloniser without Ships

Here is the second sense of the title: for ten years the right of the first reflex did what the left regards as its own job. It served the part of the rural and small-town working class that the liberal left is repelled by and ashamed of: people with guns, with a church, with a flag on the porch, with a hierarchy in the family which they themselves regard as order. The liberal left either pretends they are not there, or is disgusted by them, or, finally, treats them with the empathy of a coloniser who is fond of the people under his care but knows better than they do what they need. Barack Obama said in 2008 of the inhabitants of small-town Pennsylvania that they get bitter and “cling to guns or religion”; the sentence was kindly meant, and that is exactly where the coloniser sits, because it explains away other people’s attachments as a symptom that will pass. The old mainstream right was honest in a different way: Mitt Romney spoke in 2012 of the forty-seven per cent whom he would “never convince that they should take personal responsibility and care for their lives”. You cannot see the coloniser, because he arrives without ships: roughly the same culture, a similar language, and on top of that a civilising mission that goes by the name of civic education. The right of the first reflex was the only one that did not shame these people. But it did not represent them; it served them, as a tavern serves a thirst: it pours what the customer wants and does not ask what will become of him in the morning. I think the only honest attitude towards this part of the working class is open disagreement with their views, a refusal to accept that part of their hierarchy of values which rests on the logic of violence, physical exploitation and coercion. What we owe these communities is to hold them to ethical expectations, even demands, but also to create the conditions in which they can be met. If part of the left would like to describe a certain level of personal ethics as a class privilege, then as a liberal I reply: in that case it is time to hand that privilege out to everyone.

Sarmatism, the self-image of the old Polish nobility, is a notion I like to return to, because I know it very well from my own part of the world, and because I believe it can help explain a good many things in the United States. I wrote here in August and in September about the Golden Liberty of a single estate and about its partition from within; today I am interested in its mentality, the Sarmatian one: aggressive ignorance; one’s own privilege taken for freedom; a sense of exceptionalism mixed with an inferiority complex and a superiority complex at once; dissent that counts as an argument because it is mine; and the conviction that repairing the system is treason against the system. Donald Trump, seen from Poznań, looks like a Polish Sarmatian: a nobleman who has everything, believes everything is owed to him, and is convinced that the world has conspired to take it away. This Sarmatian mode does not belong to one side. The right speaks it in honour and apocalypse, the liberal centre in “going high” and contempt, but these are two dialects of one language, in which the first question is who I am in relation to you, and only the second is what there is to be done.

Examination of Conscience

I would not want this essay to sound like an ode to traditional Republicans and an indictment of those who came after them. The old mainstream right was not destroyed by the right of the first reflex; it made a deal with it. Lindsey Graham wrote in May 2016 that if the party nominated Trump it would be destroyed and would deserve it, and until his death in July 2026 he was Trump’s most faithful defender; Ted Cruz, whose wife Trump had publicly insulted, endorsed him in September; Marco Rubio called him a con artist and became his Secretary of State. In 1962 William F. Buckley Jr. broke with the leader of the John Birch Society and in 1965 with the Society itself, because a movement that cannot tame its lunatic flank ceases to deserve a hearing; in 2016 his successors handed the flank the whole tent in exchange for judges and tax cuts.

Even the best version of that good old mainstream right had a limit, visible from the credo’s other two terms, the socialist and the liberal. The best conservatism of McCain, whom I pointed to here in July as a model of a functional right, of Romney and of Pence stopped, on its left side, where inequality began, because it took inequality for nature, and Kołakowski was right to write that the pessimism from which it follows, by a curious reasoning, that a progressive income tax is an inhuman abomination is just as suspect as the optimism on which the Gulag Archipelago was based; on the liberal side it ended where institutions stopped serving it. And the limits of backbone can be measured: McCain gave his thumbs-down while already dying; in 2020 Romney was the only member of his party to vote to convict, and he did not run again; on 6 January Pence presided over the count and paid for it with his career; Cruz and Rubio gave way because they had careers ahead of them, and Graham gave way first and lasted longest. Brad Raffensperger, in charge of elections in Georgia, answered the request to find 11,780 votes by saying that the numbers were what they were; he still won re-election in 2022, but this year he finished third in the primary for governor, behind two Trump-backed candidates, so he too paid. Backbone turned out, as a rule, to be a function of the distance to the next election, and an institution that relies on retirees is not an institution.

Principles That Stopped Serving

The self-styled protectors of principles, who called them the foundation, betrayed them exactly when the principles stopped serving them. Fiscal discipline: the Tea Party movement grew in 2009 out of Obama’s deficits, and the same Republican Party passed tax cuts in 2017 that added nearly $1.5 trillion to the deficit, and a bill signed on 4 July 2025 which, by the Congressional Budget Office’s reckoning, adds some $3.4 trillion to deficits by 2034. Free trade: from Reagan to NAFTA, and then, on 2 April 2025, “Liberation Day”, tariffs on the whole world. Law and order: half a century as the party of the police, and on 20 January 2025 pardons for some 1,500 people convicted over 6 January, including for beating police officers. Character: in 1998 an impeachment for perjury about an affair, in 2024 a conviction on thirty-four counts, swallowed without indignation. The Democrats too abandoned principles when they stopped serving them; but with them these were exceptions that had to be explained, whereas on the right it is the pattern in the plaster that covers the monument to Donald Trump.

What this says about Republicans interests me less than what kind of system they were building. And here I put forward a hypothesis. A rule applied only to “the others” does not have the form of a principle in Kant’s sense, a measure to which the one proclaiming it is also subject; it is a rule of prudence, team colours. Motive cannot be read off an act, so I leave aside what these people understood and look only at how the rule worked, which was as an attribute of position rather than a bond: it bound the weaker and let the stronger say one thing today and another tomorrow. The counterexample comes from the same movement, because Buckley in the 1960s applied the rule to his own, and that is how we know it could be done differently. This also explains what the right of the first reflex cannot do: it does not know how to lose, because in such a use of rules a loss is a loss of position, not the outcome of a game. The seventh of November illustrates this mechanism rather than adding to it: four days after the defeat, the loss was to be reversed with an instrument of power instead of being accepted. I suspect, though I cannot prove it, that it absorbed the lesson the left taught in universities for forty years, that every rule is a mechanism of power, and drew the opposite conclusion from it: not “therefore no rule is legitimate”, but “so how do we learn to configure the rules so that the privileged group stays in power”.

What the Right Carries

I do not want to confine myself to the custodians of conservative ideas. I assume that the poor moral and intellectual condition of that milieu is a passing phenomenon. But given the right’s present dysfunction, I speak up for five principles that, as I see it, the right itself ought to be defending; the first three are Kołakowski’s, the fourth is Burke’s, the fifth is mine.

First: there never were, and never will be, improvements in human life that do not have to be paid for by a deterioration in some other respect; innumerable evils are compatible and can be suffered at once, while many goods exclude or limit one another. When men fear equal rights for women because they fear equal competition, they are right to be afraid: it will be harder for them. The reasons women should have equal rights are incomparably weightier than that fear, and to yield to it would be a crime; but the rightness of a change does not abolish its cost, somebody bears it, and if nobody tells him so at the very start, then one day he will hear it from someone who will turn it into a slogan and a tale of a left-liberal conspiracy.

Competition comes from scarcity, not from capitalism, and in the country where I was born the communist authorities, from the mid-1960s and more generously after 1968, awarded points at university entrance exams for working-class and peasant origin, because the competition for places was just as fierce, only the party chose its criteria; Kołakowski himself writes, in the liberal part of the credo, that a society in which all forms of competition have been done away with will not keep the incentives for creativity and progress. A conservative has a natural reflex to count that cost; in his mature form he counts it without questioning the change, and in his immature form he makes it a reason to reverse the change. The Republican custodians sold out this thesis in both directions. They denied that the cost exists: they declared tariffs pure gain, and when, after 28 February, petrol went from $2.98 to more than $4, the President wrote in March that higher oil prices were “a very small price to pay” for safety and peace, and in October said of the American oil industry: “we’re making a freaking fortune”; on the evening after the defeat he said in one interview that the election had been lost on petrol prices, not on the war, and in another, the same evening, that Iran had been a piece of it, as if the one were not the consequence of the other.

Second: we do not know to what extent inherited forms of life, family, nation, religious communities, rituals, are indispensable to the survival of societies and to the quality of that survival; there are arguments for fighting some religious practices where they do psychological or physical harm, but even then one has to ask what the form carried and what its removal will cost.

The conservative asks what will happen when a given form is gone. The liberal adds the question whether the form can be justified. The American republic stood on a few such forms, which had faded somewhat because they fell victim to their own success. For more than a century they worked, though for a long time not for everyone: the loser accepted the result, nobody prosecuted the other side for what it did with its victory, and votes were counted, not negotiated. On 6 January 2021 the first of these rules, the one about accepting the result, was broken, and only then did it become clear how much had rested on it. On 7 November 2026, four days after the defeat, the President called on the Department of Justice to deal with the winners, and broke the second, the one about not prosecuting the other side. The party that was supposed to guard the forms betrayed them.

Third: the belief that envy, the craving for distinction, greed and aggression are merely the result of faulty institutions and will disappear once those are changed is an Enlightenment superstition, contrary to experience and ruinous, because whoever expects that brotherhood can be institutionalised already has a reliable blueprint for despotism.

The fourth is Burke’s, from 1790: society is a contract between the living, the dead and the unborn, and the present generation is a tenant in it, not an owner. That contract reaches deeper than Burke supposed, because it begins below the level of generations, in a single body. Derek Parfit showed in 1984 that what connects me today with me in thirty years is a matter of degree and weakens; from this he drew the conclusion that great imprudence towards one’s future self is a harm done to someone else, and also an impersonal conclusion, that one’s own self deserves less weight. I carry this, on my own account now, from the scale of the body to the scale of the state, and the transfer is conservative not by way of Burke but by the form of the obligation. Liberal self-ownership turns here into tenancy, and tenancy assumes that there is something one may not use up, though it lies in one’s hands. If my future self is to that degree someone else, then caring for it is not prudence but altruism towards someone who will inherit my decisions and whom I shall not ask for consent; diet and public debt are thus the same relation on two scales, because in both the present decides what someone without a voice will receive. The Republicans, those of the old mainstream in 2017 and those of the first reflex in 2025, behaved like Burkean tenants who came to believe they were the owners. So they betrayed conservatism once again.

The fifth is mine, and it concerns closure. In a healthy society someone must perform the function of opening and someone the function of closing. The left opens: every form is negotiable, every question may be asked anew. The right closes: certain questions are settled, the dead have claims on the living, and a community has a right to set limits to its attention. Liberalism guards choice: whether a participant can refuse, challenge the rule and leave. These are functions, not definitions of the traditions; each of the three has, in its history, also done the work of the other two, and each, carried to the absolute, turns into its own opposite. Opening without limit becomes an absence of distinctions: when everything is negotiable, nothing differs from anything else and there is nothing left to decide, so the most open society is the one in which nothing can be resolved. Closure without a condition becomes a dogma that forbids the very question it grew out of, and so loses what it was meant to guard, because a form one is no longer allowed to understand ceases to be a form and becomes a habit. The protection of choice without content becomes a freedom with nowhere to exit to: the loser may refuse, but the refusal changes nothing, so the freest is the one with the least to choose. Any particular point of closure can be rejected, but the need for closure itself cannot, because whoever wants to go somewhere must have something from which to measure the distance. Conservatism adds to this the rule of the burden of proof: whoever dismantles an institution older than himself must justify doing so, not because the old is good, but because dismantling is easy and rebuilding often impossible, since together with the institution go the practical knowledge, the web of relationships and the trust that allowed it to work.

But for closure to differ from dogma it must meet one condition: it closes for now, not for ever, and it names what would require reopening.

The five theses are, in the end, five questions that someone in a society has to keep asking so that everyone else can safely get on with other questions: what does this cost and who will pay; what happens when this form is gone; what in a human being will stay the same after the best reform; to whom will we hand what we are using up today; and which matters may, for a time, be treated as settled. None of these questions is the property of the party that lost on 3 November, and none loses its validity because the people who were supposed to ask them stopped asking them of themselves. To throw them away because the custodians proved unworthy would be to concede that the truth about cost, about form, about the human being, about the successor and about the limit belonged to them, and not to all of us.

items.articleBody:
Apple hat mit dem neuen Smart-Home-Display HomeView einen ungewöhnlichen Rekord aufgestellt: Kein anderes Apple-Produkt lässt sich bislang so stark dimmen. Das bestätigte Matthew Costello, Apples Vice President of Hardware Engineering, in einem Interview mit TechRadar anlässlich des HomeView-Marktstarts.

Das 7-Zoll-Display des HomeView kann seine Helligkeit automatisch auf gerade einmal 0,3 Nits reduzieren. Damit eignet sich das Gerät besonders für den Einsatz auf dem Nachttisch, da es selbst in dunklen Räumen nur sehr wenig Licht abgibt. Zum Vergleich: Aktuelle iPhones und das iPad mini erreichen bei minimaler Helligkeit rund ein Nit.

Display für Tag und Nacht

Der Apple HomeView hat kürzlich nicht nur seinen Verkaufsstart, sondern direkt auch einen neuen Rekord gefeiert. Bei maximaler Helligkeit erreicht der Bildschirm 500 Nits. Nachts kann das Gerät auf 0,3 Bits herunter dämmen. Die automatische Anpassung soll dafür sorgen, dass HomeView sowohl tagsüber als auch nachts angenehm genutzt werden kann. Costello bezeichnete das Gerät scherzhaft als das am stärksten abgedimmte Produkt in Apples gesamtem Portfolio.

Im Interview betonte der Apple-Manager außerdem, dass HomeView von Anfang an rund um Siri AI entwickelt wurde. Die Benutzeroberfläche sei speziell auf die Nutzung im Haushalt zugeschnitten. Persönliche Informationen und relevante Anwendungen sollen automatisch für die jeweils erkannte Person angezeigt werden. Verlässt diese den Bereich des Geräts, verschwinden ihre persönlichen Inhalte wieder vom Bildschirm.

Mit HomeView will Apple eine neue zentrale Anlaufstelle für die Steuerung des vernetzten Zuhauses schaffen. Das Gerät ist seit dem 13. November in ausgewählten Ländern erhältlich und kostet in den USA 299 Dollar. In der Europäischen Union ist es wegen der bislang fehlenden Siri-AI-Unterstützung vorerst nicht verfügbar. Wir können uns gut vorstellen, dass Apple HomeView ab März / April auch in der EU erhältlich sein wird. Wir hoffen zumindest, dass sich Apple und die EU bis dahin auf einen Start von Siri AI auf dem iPhone, iPad und der Apple Watch einigen können.

items.articleBody:
Tree trunks puncture the slim timber platforms of this minimalist sauna in a Japanese woodland, designed by local architecture studio Daichi Inc.

Named Daichi Silent River Tree Sauna, the project is nestled within a forest in Kanagawa, southwest of Tokyo, and forms part of the Daichi Silent River retreat alongside guest cabins and additional sauna spaces.

Gallery

Previous

Next

Gallery

Close

Site plan

Plan

Roof plan

Section

According to Daichi Inc, the idea for the project was to make the trees feel "part of the architecture itself", using them as both supports and the defining feature of the pared-back structure.

The sauna has been shortlisted in the Leisure and wellness category of Dezeen Awards 2026.

"Conventional architecture typically clears nature away, cutting down thick and strong trees and transforming them into standardised building materials," said the studio.

"In this project, however, the existing trees were preserved and used directly as part of the spatial framework, blurring the boundary between nature and the built environment," it added.

"Rather than placing architecture on top of nature, the project allows architecture to coexist with it, creating an immersive bodily experience in which people feel as though they are dissolving into the forest itself."

Daichi Silent River Tree Sauna's structure comprises two stacked timber decks and a roof, with the central platform partially supported by the site's natural slope.

The thin planes sit atop timber grids supported by the trees themselves and punctured by small circular cut-outs through which their trunks can grow.

Timber steps connect these different platforms, culminating on the upper level where the central sauna room sits, wrapped in frameless glass panels. It contains a wooden bench and a central log burner.

Aside from the sauna room and a small plunge pool, the decks are left entirely open and flexible, and are surrounded by slender metal balustrades at their edges.

"Wood and glass were used as the primary materials, while the existing trees themselves were integrated into the architectural framework," said the studio.

Read:

Charred tree trunks support sauna on Finnish island by Jaakko Torvinen

"Decks and sauna spaces were carefully positioned to appear as if floating within the forest," it added. "The forest is not treated as a backdrop, but functions as an essential structural part of the architecture itself

Other saunas recently featured on Dezeen include Puusauna in Finland by architect Jaakko Torvinen, which is supported by whole, charred tree trunks sourced from the neighbouring forest, and an off-grid bathhouse in London.

items.subtitle: Portrait of Abraham Lincoln.

items.articleBody:
Portrait of Abraham Lincoln. (Photo: PHOTOGRAPHER/AUTHOR'S NAME via Wikimedia Commons, Public domain)

For nearly 90 years, a damaged glass plate negative concealed a remarkable piece of American history. Cataloged as a crowd scene, the photograph showed spectators gathered around a platform in Gettysburg, Pennsylvania. In 1952, archivist Josephine Cobb enlarged the image and discovered Abraham Lincoln standing among the crowd. The photograph captured the president at the dedication of the Soldiers’ National Cemetery on November 19, 1863, the same day he delivered the Gettysburg Address.

Cobb joined the U.S. National Archives in 1936. Her work focused on historical photographs, including Civil War images. When she examined the glass plate, she suspected it might depict the Gettysburg ceremony. A tall flag helped her locate the speakers’ platform. She then enlarged that section to examine the figures more closely.

The result revealed a small, bare-headed man with a beard and a distinctive profile. Cobb identified him as Lincoln. She also recognized Ward Hill Lamon, the president’s bodyguard and the ceremony’s chief marshal, along with Pennsylvania Governor Andrew Curtin. Other figures have been proposed as members of Lincoln’s party, though some identifications remain disputed.

The photograph belonged to a collection associated with Civil War photographer Mathew Brady. The U.S. government purchased Brady’s photographic collection in the 1870s, and the material eventually entered the National Archives. However, the photographer who took this particular image remains unknown. The glass plate had also lost roughly a quarter of its upper-left corner, further complicating its examination.

Cobb estimated that the photograph was taken around noon, when Lincoln arrived at the platform. His famous address came approximately three hours later. The image does not capture the speech itself. Instead, it offers a rare glimpse of Lincoln at the ceremony before he delivered one of the most enduring speeches in American history.

The discovery became public on February 12, 1953, Lincoln’s birthday. The Gettysburg Times reported the finding, and Life magazine later published the image. Early coverage approached the identification cautiously because the figure’s face was blurred. Lincoln occupies only a small portion of the original photograph, making historical context essential to the identification.

Cobb’s discovery reflected years of experience examining archival images. Her work illustrates why historical photographs deserve more than a cursory glance. A vague catalog entry had obscured the significance of the Gettysburg image for decades. By questioning its description and carefully examining the evidence, Cobb brought a long-overlooked piece of history into view.

In 1952, National Archives archivist Josephine Cobb enlarged a damaged glass plate negative and discovered Abraham Lincoln in a crowd at Gettysburg.

A modern enlargement printed from the original glass plate, held by the Library of Congress and shown in its American Treasures exhibit. Lincoln is the hatless, bearded figure just left of center; the Library lists John Hay, John Nicolay, Edward Everett and Gettysburg attorney David Wills among the surrounding figures scholars have argued over. Photographer attributions vary from unidentified to Mathew Brady to David Bachrach. (Photo: Library of Congress, Public domain)

The photograph captures Lincoln at the November 19, 1863, cemetery dedication, hours before he delivered the Gettysburg Address.

Crowd of citizens, soldiers, and etc. with Abraham Lincoln at Gettysburg. (Photo: National Archives Catalog, Public domain)

Mislabeled for nearly 90 years, the photograph was identified through Cobb’s research and careful examination of the original glass plate.

Cobb in the Still Picture stacks, holding a Brady photograph of the 20th Maine Infantry Regiment, with Brady portraits of Abraham Lincoln and Hannibal Hamlin on the shelf behind her. The Archives caption on the print calls her Archivist in Charge of the Still Picture Branch. (Photo: National Archives Catalog, Public domain)

items.articleBody:
**Diese Woche wird es in drei Richtungen gleichzeitig spannend. Overtonium von Dehli Musikk ist ein Additiv-Synth, der aussieht wie ein 32-Kanal-Mischpult und jeden einzelnen Oberton auf die Oberfläche holt. Ultiverb von Libelula Audio ist eines der funktionsreichsten kostenlosen Reverbs, die wir bisher gezeigt haben. Und ENS-86 von Hivetune bringt den klassischen BBD-Chorus der Achtziger in die DAW. Alles kostenlos, alles mit eigenem Kopf. Falls ihr darüber hinaus auf der Suche nach weiteren Freeware Plugins seid, [schaut mal in unserer Sammlung vorbei!](https://www.gearnews.de/besten-freeware-plugins-synthesizer-recording/)**

## Kostenlose Plugins zum Freeware Sonntag

- Dehli Musikk Overtonium: Additive Synthese zum Anfassen
- Libelula Audio Ultiverb: Das ultimative kostenlose Reverb?
- Hivetune ENS-86: Kostenloser Chorus im BBD-Stil
- Weitere Freebies wie Overtonium, Angebote und Tipps & Tricks…

## Dehli Musikk Overtonium: Additive Synthese zum Anfassen

Den Rekord für die meisten Regler in einem Plugin hat vermutlich gerade jemand geknackt. Overtonium von [Dehli Musikk](https://www.gearnews.de/hersteller/dehli-musikk/) ist ein Additiv-Synthesizer, der „ein Regler pro Funktion“ ziemlich wörtlich nimmt. Das Layout erinnert an ein 32-Kanal-Mischpult. Andere Additiv-Synths verstecken ihre Partials gern hinter Makro-Reglern, Overtonium legt sie alle offen auf den Tisch und gibt euch Zugriff auf jeden einzelnen Oberton.

Jeder Kanal in Overtonium gibt eine Sinuswelle aus, die einer Harmonie des gespielten Tons entspricht. Jedes Partial lässt sich einzeln stimmen (für unterschiedliche Temperierungen), im Panorama platzieren, muten und solo schalten. Das ist aber erst der Anfang: Pro Partial gibt es eine eigene Modulationssektion mit Pitch-LFO, Amp-LFO und ADSR-Hüllkurvengenerator. Rechts sitzt ein zusätzlicher Kanal mit Rauschen, oben im GUI warten Effekte wie Character, Echo und Reverb.

Wer schon immer wissen wollte, wie additive Synthese eigentlich funktioniert, findet kaum eine übersichtlichere Lernhilfe wie mit Overtonium. Und klingen tut das Ganze auch, vor allem mit expressiver MPE-Steuerung. Sehr schön!

Im Studio lohnt sich ein ungewöhnlicher Einstieg: Schaltet zuerst fast alle Partials im Dehli Musikk Overtonium stumm und holt sie nacheinander dazu. So hört ihr ziemlich gut, wie sich eine einfache Sinuswelle nach und nach verändert. Mit den passenden Einstellungen entsteht daraus beispielsweise ein Orgelklang. Auch glockenartige Sounds sind möglich. Für Pads würde ich die höheren Partials mit längeren Decay- und Release-Zeiten versehen. Dadurch entwickelt sich der Klang weiter, während ihr weiterhin eure Finger auf der Taste haltet.

Dehli Musikk Overtonium ist für **macOS**,**Windows**und**Linux**in den Formaten**VST3**,**AU**und**LV2** erhältlich.

- [Hier geht’s zum Download](https://benjamindehli.github.io/overtonium/)
- [Mehr von Dehli Musikk](https://www.gearnews.de/hersteller/dehli-musikk/)

## Libelula Audio Ultiverb: Das ultimative kostenlose Reverb?

Noch ein kostenloser Hall, könnte man denken. Ultiverb von [Libelula Audio](https://www.gearnews.de/hersteller/libelula-audio/) belehrt einen schnell eines Besseren, denn das ist eines der funktionsreichsten Freeware-Reverbs, die mir bisher untergekommen sind. Fast jeder Aspekt des Halls lässt sich sehr detailliert steuern, von den Grundparametern bis zu präziser Klangformung und kreativem Sounddesign.

In der Space-Sektion stehen fünf Algorithmen für grundverschiedene Hallarten bereit: Room, Hall, Plate, Spring und Digital. Den Hall stellt ihr zunächst über die bekannten Parameter ein. Decay Time bestimmt die Nachhallzeit, mit Size verändert ihr die Raumgröße. Dazu kommen Pre-Delay, Diffusion und Early Reflections. Vier unterschiedliche „Flavors“ verleihen dem Hall dann noch einen eigenen Charakter.

Libelula Audio Ultiverb · Quelle: Libelula Audio

Aber das ist längst nicht alles. Ultiverb erlaubt euch, die Decay-Zeiten für verschiedene Frequenzbänder getrennt einzustellen. Damit könnt ihr beispielsweise verhindern, dass sich zu viel Hall im Bassbereich ansammelt. Die Sektionen Motion und Fluctuate bringen zusätzlich Bewegung ins Spiel. Letztere soll für eine gewisse analoge Unvollkommenheit sorgen. Auch getrennte Sättigungsstufen für das Dry- und Wet-Signal sind integriert. Und einen Ducker gibt es ebenfalls. Wie bitte? Genau, das alles kostenlos.

Im Studio finde ich vor allem die getrennten Decay-Zeiten interessant. Ich würde den Hall im unteren Frequenzbereich deutlich kürzer einstellen, damit Vocals oder Snares nicht unnötig zugeschmiert werden. Die hohen Frequenzen lasse ich dagegen gerne etwas länger ausklingen. Sehr interessant ist natürlich der integrierte Ducker. Gerade bei euren Vocals ist das eine ziemlich coole Sache, denn der Hall wird automatisch in der Lautstärke leider geregelt, sobald gesungen wird. In den Gesangspausen kommt er dann natürlich wieder nach vorne und ist hörbar.

Schade ist (gerade für mich), dass Libelula Audio Ultiverb zurzeit nur für **Windows**als**VST3**erhältlich ist. Wer wie ich am**Mac** arbeitet, schaut erst einmal in die Röhre. Immerhin könnt ihr euch auf der Website des Entwicklers in eine Warteliste eintragen. Sobald die Mac-Version erscheint, erhaltet ihr eine Nachricht.

- [Hier geht’s zum Download](https://libelula-audio.com/en/plugins/ultiverb/)
- [Mehr von Libelula Audio](https://www.gearnews.de/hersteller/libelula-audio/)

## Hivetune ENS-86: Kostenloser Chorus im BBD-Stil

ENS-86 von [Hivetune](https://www.gearnews.de/hersteller/hivetune/) emuliert die klassischen analogen BBD-Chorus-Effekte der Achtziger. Bei den alten bekannten Chorus-Effekten waren die Einstellmöglichkeiten sehr begrenzt. Hier beim Plugin sieht das glücklicherweise anders aus. Ihr könnt nicht nur die Geschwindigkeit und Intensität der Modulation verändern, sondern sogar die LFO-Phase perfekt einstellen. Über diese LFO-Phase könnt ihr einstellen, wie die Modulation auf dem linken und rechten Kanal arbeitet. Das ist gerade bei einem Chorus-Effekt sehr interessant, denn schon kleine Änderungen dieses Parameters können das Stereobild extrem interessant beeinflussen.

Hivetune ENS-86: Kostenloser Chorus im BBD-Stil · Quelle: Hivetune

Das Plugin betrachtet zudem Mid/Side getrennt, was mir ebenso sehr zusagt. Das hat natürlich mit der eigentlichen Chorus-Modulation erst einmal nichts zu tun. Aber ihr könnt den Sound damit komplett auf Mono ziehen oder die Breite auf bis zu 200 Prozent aufdrehen, also den Sound perfekt in euren Song einfügen. Für ein kostenloses Plugin finde ich das ziemlich ordentlich.

Als allererstes würde ich mit dem Tool Pads bearbeiten und mir anhören, wie weit sich der Sound im Stereobild auseinanderziehen lässt. Bei E-Pianos kann ich mir den Effekt ebenfalls sehr gut vorstellen. Dieser Effekt ist prädestiniert für solche Instrumente.

Synth-Bässe sind dagegen so eine Sache. Denn gerade im Subbereich möchte ich persönlich nicht zu viel Bewegung im Stereobild haben. Deshalb würde ich die Modulation hier eher sparsam einsetzen und anschließend mit dem Mid/Side-Regler ein wenig herumexperimentieren. Wichtig ist dabei immer der Monocheck. Wenn euch plötzlich der Subbass wegbricht, war es vermutlich etwas zu viel des Guten.

Hivetune ENS-86 ist für **macOS**und**Windows**in den Formaten**VST3**und**AU** erhältlich.

- [Hier geht’s zum Download](https://www.hivetune.com/store/ens-86/)
- [Mehr von Hivetune](https://www.gearnews.de/hersteller/hivetune/)

# Wenn den Jungen die Zukunft nur noch trostlos erscheint

© unsplash Wenn junge Menschen aus der Peripherie die Zentren großer Städte heimsuchen, um mit Gewalt und Plünderungen Angst und Schrecken zu verbreiten, dann kann das selten eindimensional erklärt werden. Doch als Fundament für die desolate Lage dient eine Betrachtung der Einkommensstatistik. Das gilt für Frankreich, aber auch für Italien, wo die Proteste ähnlich ausgeartet sind wie im Nachbarland, wenn auch auf niedrigerem Niveau: Zwischen 2019 und 2026 sind die durchschnittlichen Reallöhne in keinem anderen EU-Land so stark gesunken wie in Italien, nämlich um 3,9 Prozent. Es gab zwar Steigerungen, doch noch immer haben die Menschen, gemessen an der Inflation, weniger Einkünfte als vor der Pandemie.

Es dürfte kein Zufall sein, dass Frankreich das Land mit der zweitschlechtesten Lohnentwicklung der EU ist. Dort liegen die Reallöhne mit 2,4 Prozent unter dem Niveau von 2019. Daneben gibt es nur zwei weitere Länder, in denen der Reallohn in diesen sieben Jahren sank, jedoch nur minimal: in Finnland um minus 1,3 Prozent sowie in Griechenland um minus 0,1 Prozent. Alle anderen 23 EU-Staaten erlebten meist deutliche Reallohnsteigerungen seit dem letzten Vorpandemiejahr; in 13 Ländern waren es mehr als fünf Prozent.

## Alte Probleme sind geblieben

Die Zahlen stammen aus dem Ausblick auf Beschäftigung und soziale Entwicklung, den die EU-Kommission in diesem Monat veröffentlicht hat. Weite Teile der italienischen Bevölkerung haben mit materieller Stagnation zu kämpfen, darunter viele junge Menschen. Die italienische Volkswirtschaft kennzeichnen geringe Löhne schon lange, was oft mit kleinen Produktivitätsfortschritten erklärt wurde. Der Druck kumuliert sich, sodass er sich irgendwann entlädt. Trotz gewisser Wachstumserfolge der Regierung von Giorgia Meloni seit ihrer Wahl vor vier Jahren haben sich die Einnahmen real wenig verbessert, denn die Inflation fraß immer wieder alles auf. Alte Probleme sind geblieben wie geringe Unternehmensgrößen, schwache Innovationsinvestitionen, Spezialisierung auf Branchen mit niedriger Wertschöpfung sowie veraltete Tarifverträge infolge verhärteter Fronten zwischen Gewerkschaften und Unternehmen.

So stiegen die durchschnittlichen Nominallöhne im italienischen Privatsektor zwischen 2015 und 2025 zwar um fast 21 Prozent und im öffentlichen Dienst um gut 16 Prozent. Doch angesichts einer kumulierten Inflation von 24,2 Prozent in diesen zehn Jahren blieb den Haushalten am Ende weniger als zuvor.

## „Mangel an Werten und Zukunftsperspektiven“

Schon auf dem Bildungsweg führt dies bei vielen jungen Menschen in Italien zu einer gefühlten Aussichtslosigkeit, die in Wut umschlagen kann. „Die Schule ermöglicht nicht mehr wie früher den gesellschaftlichen und wirtschaftlichen Aufstieg“, erklärt Giovanni Diamanti, Dozent an der Universität Padua und Mitgründer des Umfrageunternehmens Youtrend, in der Zeitung „Il Messaggero“. „Die Ungleichheiten nehmen zu, und junge Menschen wandern aus, weil sie für die Miete ihr gesamtes Einkommen ausgeben müssen.“ Bei Einwanderern, auch der zweiten oder dritten Generation, kommt das Gefühl oder das tatsächlich erlittene Leid der Diskriminierung hinzu.

Neben einer Mehrheit friedlicher Demonstranten mit legitimen Forderungen nach besseren Lern- und Studienbedingungen, Gehältern und Jobaussichten ist eine Gruppe schwer erreichbarer Jugendlicher herangewachsen. Viele sind von den sozialen Medien stärker geprägt als von ihren Elternhäusern. Politische Motive sind allenfalls diffus vorhanden, wenn überhaupt. „Das Grundproblem bei den rebellischen Jugendlichen ist die Apathie gegenüber der Politik. Sie haben es vor allem auf hochwertige Güter wie Markenkleidung abgesehen, die außerhalb ihrer Reichweite liegen. Hinzu kommt ein umfassender Mangel an Werten und Zukunftsperspektiven“, meint Diamanti.

## Relativ wenige Italiener gehen an die Uni

Was nach der Schule kommt, ist für viele junge Menschen in Italien ungewiss. Die Jugendarbeitslosigkeit sank seit Mitte des vergangenen Jahrzehnts zwar deutlich, doch sie gehört mit zuletzt gut 20 Prozent immer noch zu den schlechtesten Werten Europas. Laut OECD hatten 2025 fast 16 Prozent der 18- bis 24-Jährigen keine Arbeit oder Ausbildung. Der Durchschnitt der 38 OECD-Länder liegt bei gut 14 Prozent.

Die Universität zu besuchen, verspricht nicht unbedingt eine bessere Zukunft, zudem schlagen viele Italiener diesen Weg gar nicht ein. Italien rangiert in der Altersklasse 25 bis 34 Jahre beim Anteil der Menschen mit Hochschulbildung auf dem vorletzten Rang der EU. Viele Studenten brauchen auch lange bis zum Abschluss oder steigen vorher aus. Im Jahr 2023 schafften fast 44 Prozent der Bachelor-Studenten den Abschluss nicht in den meist vorhergesehenen drei Jahren, berichtet die EU-Kommission. 40 Prozent der Uni-Abgänger arbeiten in Jobs, die nichts mit ihrem Studium zu tun haben.

Dass der italienische Staat seinen Bildungsauftrag nur unzureichend erfüllt, lässt sich auch an den Ausgaben ablesen. Für Schulen und Universitäten gibt Italien laut OECD nur 3,4 Prozent des Bruttoinlandsproduktes aus, während der OECD-Durchschnitt bei 4 Prozent liegt. Das Lehrpersonal ist schlecht bezahlt, zudem sind die Professoren und Dozenten an den italienischen Universitäten im Durchschnitt so alt wie in keinem anderen EU-Land. Die Investitionen im Zuge des während der Pandemie beschlossenen EU-Wiederaufbauplanes brachten zwar etwas Linderung, doch immer noch befinden sich etliche Schulen und Unis in einem schlechten baulichen Zustand und leiden unter Personalmangel sowie einer schleppenden Bürokratie.
